speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend reminds the house, this question was asked yesterday. The decision of the Greek government to withdraw elements of its land, air and naval forces from NATO was officially made known to the NATO authorities yesterday afternoon. Members of the house will recall that action of a similar nature, relating to air force units only, however, had been taken earlier by Turkey.
The Canadian government regrets that both these governments should have found it necessary, for national purposes, to remove forces which had been assigned as part of NATO's defensive strength. However, the matter is now being discussed in NATO and I do not feel I can go any further at this time.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the minister can tell us whether the Greeks have withdrawn the major portion of their forces from NATO, or only a small portion; and particularly whether the withdrawal of the Greek portion of the eastern Mediterranean headquarters at Izmir means that this will now cease to be an effective NATO eastern Mediterranean headquarters.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. In answer to the last question, there is no word of developments of that kind. The full extent of the withdrawal is now a matter of discussion, however, in the NATO council.

I have a supplementary question for the minister, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the minister can tell us whether it is the intention of the government to recall to Canada the Canadian air force officers who are serving with the Turkish air force at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Perhaps I might answer that question, Mr. Speaker. The house has already been informed that shipments of mutual aid in respect of aircraft parts to both Greece and Turkey have been suspended. Previously, in order to facilitate the supply of spares and the return of equipment to Canada for repair, we had officers in both Greece and Turkey. Some time ago the office in Greece was with-


drawn. This was in accordance with previous plans. The office in Turkey was given responsibility for liaison with both the Turkish air force and the royal Hellenic air force. They have been instructed, however, to cease visits pending further developments.
There are three service personnel, one squadron leader and two sergeants, and two contract field service representatives, one Canadair and one Rolls Royce, remaining in Turkey. All these people's tours expire within the next few months and they will not be replaced at that time, unless there is a stabilization of the situation in the meantime. One officer, who had just returned to Canada when his tour expired, was not replaced. That is the situation at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, could I ask the minister whether any of the 107 Sabre jets which Canada gave to Turkey were used by that nation in the recent bombing raids on Cyprus?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I could deal with this particular question, Mr. Speaker. With regard to the recent press report that Turkey, and perhaps also Greece, used Canadian built aircraft provided to them as mutual aid in Cyprus, the position on F-104's was given in detail by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, as the hon. gentleman will recall, on May 13 this year.
With regard to the F-86 aircraft, Canada undertook in 1954 a program for the provision of F-86 mark II aircraft to Greece and also to Turkey under the general program for the provision of mutual aid to NATO countries. In all some 107 aircraft were provided to each country, with spare engines and spares support. There have been reports in the papers that F-86 aircraft were used by both Greece and Turkey during recent days, but we are not in a position as of this moment to know whether such aircraft had in fact been supplied by Canada several years ago under the NATO arrangements for the mutual assistance program.
However, I should point out to the house that equipment given by Canada as mutual aid is provided on the condition that the recipient nation accepts responsibility for use of the equipment so received to strengthen the capacity of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to deter or resist aggression. The implications of this condition in the present circumstances are being brought again to the attention of the governments involved. As my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence pointed out, at the

time when Canada decided to take part in the United Nations force in Cyprus there was a suspension by Canada of its mutual aid assistance program to Greece and Turkey.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. Could I ask the minister what steps the Canadian government takes to see that the recipients of military material, such as planes, use that material for the purpose for which it was intended; and in the event that the government finds it is not used for that purpose, is it the government's intention to have the material returned to Canada?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if it were confirmed that these planes had been used contrary to the requirement of use, the Canadian government would raise the matter at once in the NATO council.

The house resumed, from Monday, August 17, consideration of the motion by Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, when I began my remarks last evening I mentioned that the day a nation

unfurl its new flag should be a time of excitement and enthusiasm; it should be a time when the various divisive elements become united and stand behind the new flag, the new symbol which everyone can accept.
That this is not possible at this time should be patently clear to the house. We hear some very sincere, vintage speeches being made by hon. members on this side of the house, but we notice a surprising poverty of speeches from the other side of the house. I am wondering why this is so. Can this be because there is a lack of conviction on the part of hon. members on the other side of the house who are being asked to support a flag for which they cannot quite speak up? Can it be that there is an unwillingness on their part to do so because of the feeling that their constituencies might have them do otherwise? Why is there no enthusiastic response to defend the flag?
I think of some of the very notable speeches that have come from this side of the house, and I noticed hon. members opposite listening with great interest to the very reasonable and reasoned arguments that were undoubtedly put forward. I am just wondering why the indifferent attitude of hon. members opposite is so evident and why they cannot be persuaded by this kind of reasoning. Surely the Prime Minister himself must be quite chagrined over the turn of events since the introduction of the main motion, a motion that he hoped would bring about national unity but which has now brought about the greatest division in our country that we can remember.
With regard to this very point of national unity, Mr. Speaker, I would think all members on all sides of the house are certainly anxious to strive for and do all those things that will contribute to national unity. For this reason I fail to understand why, when a reasonable suggestion is put forward, such as has been made by the Leader of the Opposition, to put this question before the people of Canada in the form of a referendum, the suggestion cannot be accepted. Surely this is a nation-saving move, an excellent and honourable way for the Prime Minister to get out of the dilemma in which he now finds himself.
In this tenth day of debate of this issue there is, I can assure the house, no less enthusiasm for speakers on this side of the house to defend the actions taken by earlier speakers or to defend the measures that will really bring about the national unity that
Canadian Flag
we all expect. I have mentioned the lack of speakers from the other side of the chamber. One hon. member said this reminds him of a lawyer appearing in court with no witnesses. Why is this so? Is he unable to bring witnesses? Are hon. members opposite unable to muster arguments in the defence of their choice of a national flag?
I believe that members on all sides of the house must be receiving the kind of mail that we on this side are receiving. I cannot accept that merely because my neighbour happens to be in another political party the residents of that constituency are not writing the kind of letters that I and other hon. members are receiving. This makes me believe that hon. members who are not willing to tell the house of the kind of letters they are receiving are simply unable to do so because they are not in accord with the main motion put to the house by the Prime Minister.
As my witness I would call an editorial appearing in the Daily Graphic of May 21. This newspaper enjoys a wide circulation in my riding. The editorial reads in part as follows:
The Canadian people have never been directly asked if they want a new flag. Surely this is the first step; it seems to us the question should be asked directly, in a national referendum, and not in the conflict of a partisan election.
If we give birth to a flag out of today's dissension, by a pressed vote in parliament, what will it mean? Further dissension, undoubtedly.
Consider, instead, with what pride and fanfare a flag ... and maybe a better flag ... might have been produced by a dominion-provincial conference that will, in due course, have to consider constitutional changes.
Today is hardly the time, in the face of angry dissension, to force the flag issue on the Canadian people.
I believe many of us have come to feel this way, and that is why there have been repeated requests by speakers to have this matter held over for a few months so that feelings on this issue may be cooled and brought more into line. Coming to the point under discussion-to which I am sure we must limit ourselves-namely the referendum and the plebiscite itself, I would call as another witness an editorial which appeared in the Portage Leader, which says in part as follows:
Limitless debate on Canada's flag is right. ..
It would be best, of course, if the Canadian government were to give the people of the nation the privilege of voting in a plebiscite on this question.
It appears unlikely that Prime Minister Pearson is willing to extend to us this democratic luxury, but in the absence of such a plebiscite, it is then most necessary that every member-wherever seated in

Canadian Flag
the green chamber-should be allowed to express his views with all the eloquence at his command.
This we are doing at the invitation of the Prime Minister. This editorial continues:
In some matters, members of parliament have a duty to follow the program proposed by the party to which they belong and which has given them the privilege of sitting in the governing benches of the House of Commons.
Any man who sought and gained election on the strength of a pledge that he would scrap our national ensign and replace it with some other device must in honour adhere to this commitment.
How many did? ...
The vote on the flag issue should be completely free. Of course, it will not be. While Liberal members in the government benches have been promised that they will not be punished if they should rebel against the party line, they will be voting under a manifest discipline. Those Liberals who put loyalty to the flag above loyalty to the party may reasonably expect to lose favour in the party caucus.
This, however, is an issue on which individual members will prove their stature by acting independently and relying on the electorate rather than the party organization to pass judgment upon their actions.
With the New Democratic party and the Social Creditistes allied to the Liberals on the flag issue, it is expected that Mr. Pearson's pennant may gain parliamentary approval.
If it does, it will be a sad day for Canada, for many thousands of Canadians will be bitterly offended at the affront to the flag which they have saluted with great respect all their lives.
This is the sort of issue which can only lead to disunity. In our parliamentary democracy, however, the people-not the government-make the final decisions. Whether or not we have a plebiscite, the people will decide on the issue of the flag.
This is the good thing about parliamentary democracy that stems from the United Kingdom-the people can speak at least once in every five years. And they speak with thunderous authority.
I would remind the house that this question has developed at the insistence of the Prime Minister; he is the one who is inviting this discussion, and this is an indication that the Liberal government is not ready to test its popularity with the people of this country. Perhaps it is unwilling to test its stand in a referendum, and maybe that is the reason we are not being given the luxury, if I may call it that, of such a referendum.
With regard to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City, the first question reads:
1. Are you in favour of the red ensign?
We are asked to consider whether this is a proper question to appear on a plebiscite. I would merely call to mind a sample of some of the the mail which has come to me. First of all I should like to read a brief extract from a letter received from a study group in Winnipeg. One of the signatories to
[Mr. Enns.l
the letter is the mayor of Assiniboia. The letter reads in part:
The loss of the red ensign would cause a split in our nation such as we have never known before. This split added to the Pearson bicultural rift could spell the ruination of our future as a nation.
We believe that if the people of Canada fully understood the traditions represented by the symbols on the red ensign, they would overwhelmingly endorse its retention as our flag.
Were it not for the restrictive ruling made yesterday by the Chair I would have wanted to make additional comments about the meaning of a flag. However, I would refer hon. members to the excellent address of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who went to some length to explain the real purpose and meaning of our present flag.
This is a letter which I have received from McCreary, another part of my riding. It reads:
In regard to the national flag for Canada I am in favour of the red ensign. I am strongly in favour of the decision being left up to the people at the next election.
That is endorsing a referendum, and I have had numerous letters supporting the same step. I was also very interested to receive a petition from some collegiate students. About 100 names were placed on this petition from the Carberry collegiate, which puts forward in a very well worded resolution their arguments why they felt the red ensign should be retained as our national flag. Finally, on this first question I should like to mention that I received a letter from Westbourne which really is critical of any proposal for a referendum. However, it goes on to say:
I am not in favour of the tri-leaf flag. I think the red ensign does quite well-
So that even those letters which are critical of our stand-and they are not many in number-are still not in support of the proposed flag, the trifoil maple leaf design. I have mentioned the earlier speeches made in this house, and I have been most impressed by some of the arguments which have been put forward. I am hopeful that more people, as they become aware of the issues at stake, can be persuaded to think again about this very important step which the government is considering.
The second part of the plebiscite, question No. 2, reads:
Are you in favour of the red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
I have already indicated a strong preference for the red ensign, but I personally am

not inflexible in my stand. I also feel that many people across the country would quite readily accept a modification of the red ensign.
Here we have an odd situation which has developed. We have people who are very much in favour of the ensign and who say "Why all this fuss? Let us make the decision and make it final, and then stop any further debate". Then we have other people who say "Here is a new flag. This is what we want. Let us not continue needless debate; make it final and take a vote". Then again we have others who say "Why is a flag becoming a major issue in the first place, when there are more important things to discuss."
So it will be seen, Mr. Speaker, that we have unanimity across the land at least on one point, and that is impatience at the length of time it has taken to come to agreement on this issue. I suggest to the Prime Minister that if there cannot be agreement, then this is no time to pursue the matter further, and that the judgment of the government must be that the temper of the land will not allow a decision to be taken on the matter. Certainly we do not want to make a decision in haste, like some other decisions taken by the government which have not proven too helpful to the development of our national affairs.
Coming back to the question of accepting modifications to the ensign, I think this is a point which will bring us together. If those of us who favour the ensign are able to say "Yes, we will compromise on a modification", and if those who feel strongly for the maple leaf design can bring themselves to say "We will accept some change or modification to our proposal", then perhaps we can come together with regard to a modification, which is suggested in question 2 of the proposed plebiscite.
I have been reminded of some remarks made by Rev. Gordon Smyth of the Parkdale United church on the question of symbolism. He said:
It is impossible to cut symbolism out of the affairs of men and nations. The roots go deep. If a man were to resolve never to use a symbol again, he could not shake hands with a friend, put a ring on the finger of his bride, kiss his child or take a sacrament. Human nature requires symbols. The heart craves after some tangible expression of the intangible.
I suggest that the removal of symbols, which would mean removal of some of the traditions which we have come to revere, would be a serious undertaking, and that it ill behooves anyone to do this without
Canadian Flag
proper attention being paid to the matter. I also suggest that such a step should not be taken in any kind of haste. I believe Canadians generally have an abiding faith in divine Providence, and that most Canadians share a trust under the only flag they know. If we are to do away with all links with past traditions, are we thereby indicating that we have become insensitive to the prayers for guidance of God and blessing upon Queen and nation, which mark the start of every day's sitting of this house? The country which does not honour its past has no future.
I would remind hon. members of the emphasis which is placed by this parliament on tradition at the opening of every session. We look at the mace on the table before us and are impressed with the years of tradition which it represents. I am sure that no other ceremony in Canada is as colourful or as dignified as the opening of parliament at the commencement of every session, because that is a ceremony filled with tradition. I suggest to hon. members that the complete removal of those symbols which have become so meaningful on our national flag without full regard to the implications of such a step would be a very dangerous action to take, if it is ever successfully taken. I repeat that the country which does not honour its past has no future.
I would mention at this point the third question on the plebiscite, which really forms the second part of my argument. I interject here to say that I have heard it said that there are too many questions on the proposed plebiscite. It is said that if there are four questions to be answered this will defeat the possibility of any one question being answered in a clear, decisive manner. However, I suggest to the house that really the four questions fall very neatly into two parts. The first two questions deal with the red ensign and modification thereof; the second two questions, questions 3 and 4, deal with the maple leaf design and modification thereof.
Again I point to the wording of the proposed plebiscite, which refers to "among the questions to be placed before the people". It does not say that these are the only questions. Perhaps the questions could even be modified further. I find very little difficulty in supporting entirely the subamendment as it now appears.
Referring to the second half of the subamendment dealing with those questions in

Canadian Flag
respect of the maple leaf, permit me to name as my further witness a person eminent in public affairs, Dr. Eugene Forsey, who has been often quoted in this house and who reminds us all that we have at this stage accepted the fact that Canada is a bicultural country. If that is so, why then are we so anxious to change and keep out of the flag any implication or indication of this fact of biculturalism? Certainly the design as proposed gives no indication of this fact of biculturalism. As Dr. Forsey has said, every human vestige of our country and everything distinctively Canadian has been carefully excluded from this design by this legislation.
Of course we all realize that Canadians have carried the maple leaf insignia on their uniforms in times of war. However, this fact has been played up out of all proportion. The Royal Canadian Legion is aware of this fact, and what segment of the population is in a better position to appreciate it? What segment of the population deserves more respect? It is true that veterans wore the maple leaf in battle, but I am certain they were not marching under the maple leaf design but rather were marching into battle for ideals associated with the Canadian ensign, which have been lauded by so many capable speakers already.
The authority I have referred to, Dr. Eugene Forsey, and another eminent historian, Dr. Creighton, professor of history at the University of Toronto, wrote an open letter to the Prime Minister dated May 27, 1964, in which they say something about this distinctive new flag which I think should be repeated. That letter reads in part as follows:
We applaud your decision to seek a distinctive national flag for Canada, and recognize your courage in doing so. We believe, as you do, that the flag should be a source of national unity, and that it should be unmistakeably Canadian in character. However, we protest that the maple leaf flag is neither of these things. Its only advantage is that it is innocuous, that it produces tepid approval, mild disapproval, or indifference, and that it can therefore be adopted without any display of strong feeling whatever. We have a despairing feeling that this insipid flag, instead of promoting national unity, will produce only an indifferent response, and in doing so will subtly undermine the Canadian will to survive. We believe profoundly that this negative approach to our national symbols erodes our national spirit.
Later in this same letter these gentlemen state:
We believe that Canada has a distinguished culture of its own. We believe that this is a positive culture. We believe that the basis of this positive culture is a frank acceptance of both the English Canadian and the French Canadian civilizations. We believe that a distinctive Canadian flag should reflect this positive fact.
[Mr. EnnsJ
We are not in the position of a country with a revolutionary tradition, creating itself anew; we exist because we have inherited the past without a revolutionary upheaval. It is false and dispiriting to adopt a flag which subtly ignores the truth of our own nature. This is not the kind of symbol to rally a bewildered ... nation.
I think these are very eloquent arguments that we should be careful and slow in the removal of these things and the introduction of new symbols in our flag without paying due regard to the effect on the minds of the people of this country as a result of these significant changes. The adoption of a flag is not the kind of measure that can be amended from year to year. Very often we say that parliament decides an issue and the Canadian people must accept the decision of parliament, but most economic measures can be amended year by year and changed by increasing or decreasing the amount of expenditures, or by adopting new policies as for example in respect of foreign affairs. We know from our experience to date that the adoption of a national symbol on a new flag can and usually will arouse great emotional crises throughout the country. It would certainly be folly for anyone to suggest that parliament can come back in five years and improve on the flag by adding to it, changing the colour, or making some other change that might then be appropriate.
For that reason it is very important that the type of flag to be adopted is one that will really be accepted by all Canadians. I submit we will not know of this acceptance until there has been a national referendum held along the lines suggested in the subamendment now under discussion.
National unity and harmony are too important to be driven, introduced or threatened at this delicate stage of our Canadian history. I suggest that every precaution possible should be taken, in respect of any undertaking similar to the adoption of a new flag, to assure ourselves that we are helping to continue and strengthen a united nation willing to stand together regardless of the issues that face the country. I am confident that somehow this can be accomplished, but I believe this will require an honest effort on the part of all members to conduct themselves in such a manner that extreme positions will not be taken, but rather that positions of reasonableness will prevail.

I say this to my hon. friend, that it will make no difference to the votes of the people on this side of the house whether this is a free vote or whether it is a vote that may result in the defeat of the government. We believe in this flag individually.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there was a great deal of argument, when former matters were be-

Canadian Flag
tore the house, that nothing was going on that even faintly resembled a filibuster. There are a few innocents abroad who believed that. Today I do not believe anyone has any illusions about what is going on in the house. Hon. members opposite are determined to prolong this debate as long as possible and prevent parliament from acting.
Will the minister permit a question? My question is, who has charge of the business of parliament, the government or the opposition?

May I say this to my hon. friend, that if a party is determined to prolong the debate there is very little that can be done by any group, regardless of whether it is in the minority or the majority. I suggest to my hon. friend that the question of who is in control of this house may be answered by saying that the house leader attempts to lead the house, but if my right hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition does not choose to follow there is nothing he can do about it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we think about filibusters our minds go to other places where filibusters have been attempted. I want to suggest to my friends opposite-
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. There was a ruling made yesterday that speeches should be related to the subamendment. I would strongly urge Your Honour to enforce this ruling.

May I just speak to this point of order? I think it ought to be cleared up once and for all right now that I am opposed to the subamendment. I am speaking against it. Are only those in favour of it to be given the privilege of speaking on it?

I suggest that the hon. member who has the floor should contain himself. The decision of the Speaker yesterday was very definite, that the debate should be relevant to the subamendment. I suggest that all speakers be held to that ruling.
May I suggest that what I am saying is strictly relevant to the subamendment, which I contend is part of the filibuster.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: 1 rise on a point of order. I think the house would welcome a ruling as to whether a discussion of the nature of a filibuster is related to the subamendment before us.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think the ruling made yesterday by the Speaker,

and confirmed by the house, was to the effect that the debate at this particular stage should be confined to the subamendment. I would hope the minister would keep his remarks within the bounds of the ruling that the Chair made yesterday.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. May I refer, then, immediately to the subamendment. I am discussing the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City which appears on page 6808 of Hansard, and which suggests that the amendment before the house be amended by adding thereto certain words containing four questions. I am speaking to the subamendment and I am opposed to it. I am giving reasons why I am opposed to it.
Before the debate on the subamendment goes any further, or before what I contend is a filibuster proceeds any further, may I offer my friends opposite a few words of advice. I am not personally concerned about the prospect of a prolonged debate on this subamendment or a prolonged filibuster. I have been reconciled to it for some time now, so have my colleagues and so, I am convinced, have most of the members of this house. My concern, and it is a concern which I share with all thoughtful Canadians, is as to the effect the prolongation of this debate in an indefinite manner will have-
Change the business.
I am talking about the subamendment which prolongs the debate indefinitely.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Sit down.

In view of his statement regarding the filibuster, so-called, and his concern about the indefinite prolongation of this debate, can he say if he is ready to recommend that the government bring in closure in this debate?
No, Mr. Speaker, as I said I am prepared to stay here indefinitely. My concern with the indefinite prolongation of this debate by devices such as the subamendment which we are now discussing-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The interruptions are such that I am not able to hear very clearly what is being said.

Mr. Speaker, my concern with the indefinite prolongation of this debate

which this subamendment would lead to is not so much with its effect upon parliament.
I think parliament can survive a filibuster, although it certainly won't enhance its reputation; and the people of Canada won't enjoy the filibuster, but they will survive it too. But what about the party led by my right hon. friend, who unfortunately is not in his seat at the present time? I regret his absence because I do not like referring to the right hon. gentleman when he is not here, and that is the only reason I mentioned it.
How long can this party that he leads remain united if it continues to pursue what I regard as this irersponsible and desperate manoeuvre, trying to prevent parliament from reaching a decision on this vital issue by this device of subamendments and in any other way they choose to carry on the debate? There was a time when I had an admiration, a rather reluctant admiration I must say, for the Leader of the Opposition as he led his party out of the wilderness. He led it to power. He led it to one of the greatest electoral triumphs in the history of this country. In those days he proclaimed his vision of Canada. He spoke of one Canada, united and strong. He led a rejuvenated Conservative party that seemed temporarily at least to have submerged its reactionary tendencies. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, have they abandoned this prospect of a united Canada?
No.
Is this subamendment which I am debating a substitute for policy?
Yes.

That is what I have always contended, and the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) confirmed that this party opposite has no policy on the flag, when he spoke like that. Are hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly those who speak the same language as I do, prepared to see their party tom asunder and disintegrate?
Worry about your own party.
Is their party going to wither away into a regional party of reaction?

May I
ask the minister since when was he so concerned about the future of the Conservative party?

I shall answer that question directly. I have concern for it, and it is not only my concern. I have here an editorial from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, that
Canadian Flag
answers directly the question asked by my hon. friend opposite:
By pursuing its present tactics to the point of forcing an election-
And until I heard the Leader of the Opposition today welcoming an election, and with all that humility he has asserting that they were going to succeed the present government-indeed, calling for an election-I did not know whether this was true.
By pursuing its present tactics to the point of forcing an election, the Conservatives, either willingly or otherwise, would find themselves appealing to English speaking Canada only. Such a campaign would mean the defeat of the ten Conservative M.P.'s from Quebec, excepting possibly L6on Bal-cer.
The party of Macdonald and Cartier no longer would be a national party, flexible enough to accommodate all regions of the country and all segments of the electorate.
It would leave moderate Quebeckers no alternative to the Liberals and it would give-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. gentleman or yourself, sir, could inform the house whether the party of Macdonald and Cartier is found in the subamendment?

My trouble is that I do not find the party of Macdonald and Cartier in this house. That is my concern. What I would like to see is some of the spirit of Macdonald and Cartier, not a plebiscite, not a subamendment to prolong this debate. Let me read further from this editorial, because it is relative to this point:
Conservatism, the peculiarly Canadian brand of it so laboriously nurtured by Sir John A. Macdonald, and rooted in the creation of unity cut of diversity, would become-if it has not already become-the prisoner of prairie populism.
It is a bitter memory to recall that the Conservative party between 1958 and 1962 held 50 of Quebec's 75 seats. Today, it has ten and seems determined to lose those. If it does, not merely the Conservatives, but the entire nation will be the loser.
That is my answer. Mr. Speaker, as a Liberal I should not be concerned about the future of the Conservative party, but as a Canadian I am; and when I see the dissension in the ranks of the Conservative party it hurts me as a Canadian, because I want to see that party strong and united, able sometime, perhaps, to take over the government of this country again.

I assume, Mr. Speaker, from the latitude you are allowing the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this debate that all further members, so long as this subamendment is being debated, will be allowed the same latitude in covering the field.

Canadian Flag

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will deal fairly with all sides. I believe I am being relevant. I believe I have a right to say why I am strongly opposed to this subamendment. When I heard myself challenged, along with other members on this side, to get up and speak, what was I supposed to do; support the subamendment? I am strongly opposed to it, and I intend to give my reasons.
The other evening I listened to the Leader of the Opposition speaking on the television program "The Nation's Business." What interested me most about his remarks on that occasion was not his appeal to the people to write in to the government in support of the red ensign which, since my hon. friends would like relevance, is the subject of one of the questions proposed in the subamendment. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition was anticipating the motion he was going to put before the house when he appealed in advance for that sort of response, but predictably that appeal produced very little result. Certainly none of it came my way, and I consulted among my colleagues and found little response had come their way either.
That did not concern me particularly because that is what I expected, but what did concern me, and concerned me mightily, was the suggestion in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition that the fleur-de-lis should appear on the Canadian flag along with the union jack. Where did this suggestion come from? Did it come from the deskmate of the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer)? I should like to have an answer to that question. Did it come from any of the members of the Conservative party from the province of Quebec? I am sure if this suggestion had been put to any of those hon. gentlemen they would have spurned it with contempt. To the people of Quebec this suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition-and I have heard it echoed by a number of speakers on the other side, none of them French Canadians-must have appeared as a clumsy and gratuitous piece of appeasement; it must ha.'e appeared to my French Canadian friends as a bone thrown out to a troublesome minority to keep them quiet.
Does the second part of your resolution appeal to them?

Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition did not mean it that way. I give him the benefit of the doubt. But whatever he intended, that is how it appears; just plain, unadorned appeasement by one who had not

taken the trouble to understand the true sentiments and true feelings of the French speaking people of this country. I say now, to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. gentlemen opposite, let us forget about trying to appease anybody in connection with this flag. Let us all work toward a flag which is truly Canadian and which represents all of us, whatever our origin and language, a flag which symbolizes our unity, not our divisions.
Hear, hear.

In this subamendment-and I will be strictly relevant, as I have been-in the second of the questions proposed for a plebiscite, the hon. gentleman apparently was thinking of a union jack with a fleur-de-lis in the fly.
What is wrong with that?

What would this proposal
mean? To me it would not represent the unity of Canada. It would be a perpetual reminder of our divisions. Yesterday I listened to a number of speakers, taking part in the debate on the subamendment, who boasted of their British origins. I could boast like that, too. I am, I think, of pure Scottish blood, though there is perhaps a little Irish mixed in somewhere.
Unfortunately, not very much.

Perhaps that is right; I would like to have a little more. I received part of my education in Britain. My father fought in the first world war, and I certainly take second place to no one in my respect for British institutions or my dedication to the British connection. Moreover, I represent an English speaking constituency. I think I know one French speaking Canadian in that constituency, a very eminent lawyer. Other than that, I think they are all English speaking. Does this mean I should insist upon the union jack appearing in a Canadian flag?
Yes.

If that is the attitude we are never, in this country, going to get a flag which is acceptable. I am very proud of my British heritage, but I tell this house one thing I am even more proud of, and that is of being a Canadian.
Hear, hear.

As a Canadian I call upon all my fellow Canadians in this house to seek a flag which represents Canada at home and abroad. Such a flag should say, to borrow a phrase of the Prime Minister's, "I stand

for Canada". It would be a flag for all of us; for those of my background and experience, for those of Ukrainian origin, for those who came from Germany and Poland, for all the peoples who make up the mosaic of our culture.
During the last few days I have made a point of listening to the speeches made in this debate both on the subamendment and on the amendment which is still before the house and which hon. members opposite do not wish to come to a vote. I must say that all those to whom I listened spoke with great sincerity. They stated with sincerity their convictions about a Canadian flag, and this is as it should be. I have no quarrel with that; I hope I am speaking with some conviction myself now.
But as I listened to those speeches I must confess I was disappointed. Hon. gentlemen opposite spoke of their devotion to the red ensign. They spoke of the Christian symbolism of the crosses of the union jack. I listened very carefully and I was very impressed by some of the speeches, particularly those made by members from western Canada. Perhaps I have a little affinity with them because I spent the first 30 years of my life in that part of the country. But what I missed-and I hope the hon. gentlemen opposite will understand my concern-were evidences of the spirit which I believe must animate Canada, a spirit of tolerance and conciliation. The devotion of these hon. members to the red ensign, I can understand, but what I cannot understand, and what every thoughtful Canadian must deplore, are the derisive references to the proposal put forward by the Prime Minister as a design for Canada's flag.
I will never speak with disrespect or with derision about the Canadian ensign; I can assure hon. members of that. I do not think anyone in this house will do so. Regardless of the outcome of this debate, the red ensign will always have an honoured place in Canadian history. As hon. members opposite are fond of saying, many people fought and bled under that red ensign, so regardless of whether or not in continues as the flag of Canada, it will always be honoured. But to me, and to millions of Canadians who think like me-and there are millions of them, I can assure hon. members opposite-the three red maple leaves are also an honoured symbol of Canada, and my blood boils when members opposite refer to that symbol in disparaging terms. I do not need to remind them how many times we hear them refer with a
Canadian Flag
derisive note in their voices to the "Pearson pennant".
That is what it is.
There it is again. The national symbol of Canada is being treated with derision.
It is a Liberal flag.

Throughout the world, wherever Canadians travel and wherever Canadian soldiers are buried, the maple leaf stands for Canada. I feel that hon. gentlemen opposite, when they allow their partisan feelings to overcome their reason, might take care before they cast slurs on what has come to be known as a symbol of Canada throughout the ages, or throughout a hundred years, which amounts to ages in our history.
Listening to this debate on the subamendment-and 1 think this is relevant because I am referring to remarks made by hon. gentlemen on the other side when speaking on the subamendment-I was shocked as well as disappointed by the recurring theme that the proposed flag, the three maple leaf flag which is also mentioned in the subamendment, constitutes an appeasement of Quebec. This theme recurs throughout. It recurs in the letters I get. I regret to say it has also occurred and recurred in the speeches of my hon. friends opposite. If my hon. friends opposite are determined to alienate not only Quebec but millions of English speaking Canadians like myself, that is the thing to go on saying.
Hear, hear.

There is nothing whatever in the maple leaf design reminiscent of Quebec or of French Canada. The maple leaf is in fact the one generally acknowledged symbol of Canada. We have no other, and the one embodied in this resolution has the sanction of widespread acceptance and recognition. When I hear it suggested, as some hon. gentlemen opposite have suggested, that the maple leaf flag mentioned in the subamendment is appeasement of Quebec, I ask them this: Was the sovereign of the day seeking to appease Quebec when she approved the three maple leaves as the distinctive Canadian symbol on the Canadian coat of arms nearly 100 years ago? Was this appeasement of Quebec? Was King George V seeking to appease Quebec when he approved three red maple leaves as the Canadian symbol? Was the government of Canada seeking to appease Qubec when it designed the second world war discharge button with its three maple leaves? Was the

Canadian Flag
Canadian Legion seeking to appease Quebec when it adopted the maple leaf on its badge? I could go on, Mr. Speaker. This is what hon. gentlemen opposite are saying, that this is appeasement of Quebec.
Which ones? Name them.
As an English speaking Canadian representing an English speaking riding-

Mr Speaker, would the minister permit a question? I spoke for 40 minutes last night, and I never made any such statement at any time. You can count me out of that. I love Quebec as much as any other province of Canada. I hope the minister does, too, and will stop this partisan speech.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with the greatest respect to the speech of my hon. friend, as I hope he will to my speech. There was as much politics in his speech as there is in mine. I am as sincere in my remarks on the flag as was my hon. friend. He made no disparaging remarks about Quebec in his speech, and I thank him for it. As an English speaking Canadian representing an English speaking riding, I resent the implication that this flag is appeasement of Quebec. If I believed that, I would vote against the resolution.
To return, Mr. Speaker, to the words of the subamendment and the particular proposal put forward in this house by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), I do not think-I say this with all sincerity, and I am sure that anyone who looks at the proposition would agree-the proposed plebiscite with these four questions will advance the cause of the Canadian flag, nor will it advance Canadian unity. A plebiscite of this kind will do the very opposite. Everyone knows there are differences of opinion about the design of a Canadian flag; you do not have to have a plebiscite to determine that. When I consider the shades of opinion throughout the country on the flag, four questions would only begin to cover the vast panorama of ideas.
It is at least democracy.

We do not need a plebiscite to prove that we are not all agreed as to what might be a preferable flag. The argument that those who would lose in such a plebiscite would be reconciled by the knowledge that they had been voted down is certainly the most fatuous of all propositions. In my view a plebiscite, regardless of the questions- these four or any others-would only serve

to harden attitudes that up to that time had been tentative, flexible, open to persuasion and tolerant.
Mr. Speaker, there is only one way by which Canada will have a national flag, and that is by the decision of this parliament. Let us live up to our responsibilities; let us get down to the business of making a decision. I do not mind a debate, but let us not have a filibuster; let us not have indefinite debate which has no purpose other than to avoid the taking of decisions.
Then give us a free vote. It is as simple as that.

When I look back on the history of this country and at some of the great and momentous decisions that were taken, I do not find very much evidence of plebiscites. The only plebiscites that I have been able to find were not very satisfactory ones. I think we had some sort of a plebiscite on prohibition, which did not prevent anyone drinking. Then we had a plebiscite on national conscription, which I do not think did very much to cement the unity of this country.
I can imagine what Sir John A. Macdonald would have done with the idea of a plebiscite about confederation. You can just imagine the series of questions: Do you favour union of Ontario and Quebec? Do you favour union of Ontario and Quebec and the maritime provinces? Do you think Newfoundland should be in? And so on. One can imagine all the questions. Sir John A. Macdonald was a more sensible man; he knew that these great decisions are settled in parliament-and that is where this one is going to be settled.
Hear, hear.

If I may take another idol of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), did Sir Robert Borden take a plebiscite before he insisted upon the independence of Canada within the commonwealth?
Mr. Speaker, since I am brought in, does the hon. gentleman know that the Liberal party advocated a plebiscite in 1916 and 1917?
Hear, hear.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that was a little before my time.
Oh, oh.
You are out of your depth, anyway; it is away over your head.

The Prime Minister of Canada has taken the lead by proposing the resolution for a distinctive national flag in which he has endeavoured to embody Canada's national symbol. He has taken the responsible course of a responsible statesman.
Hear, hear.

I invite my hon. friends opposite, and particularly the Leader of the Opposition, to abandon their negative role, which gets its best representation by this futile subamendment and which is doing so much damage to his party, and for that reason to the country, and join with the Prime Minister in achieving another great step forward in our development as a nation.

Mr. Speaker, now that the government has taken part in this flag debate and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has said what has hung so heavily on his soul and has bothered his conscience over the last few days, I want to now take part in this debate on the flag. Regardless of what it may be called by any newspaper or any other news media, and even by the Minister of Trade and Commerce or any other member of this house, who have said this is a filibuster, I intend to take my part in this debate.
Shame.
Hear, hear.

Thus, Mr. Speaker, I want to take my rightful opportunity as a member of the House of Commons to state my view and express my opinion on this very important subject. We listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce start his speech with a lot of drivel and end up with emotion. He wanted to impress on the House of Commons and the country the fact that he held the red ensign dear to his heart, but he felt that it should be discarded and another flag substituted in its place. With regard to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the red ensign should include something of French Canada as one of the founding races in this country-the fleur-de-lis-the Minister of Trade and Commerce immediately charged that this was appeasement. I ask, appeasement to whom? Is it not appeasement to take away the union jack from the red ensign? I ask, appeasement to whom? I wish, Mr. Speaker, that the minister had not made his speech, because I had not intended to speak in this vein. I am not of British origin and I am not of French
Canadian Flag
origin; I am proud to be of Ukrainian origin and I am also a good Canadian.
It is furthest from my thoughts and mind to divide the people of this country. I think it is our duty in this House of Commons to bring people together in a democratic fashion in the best way possible. It is our duty to bring them to agreement. But we are not finding agreement in this country today. It makes me as a Canadian other than of French or English origin bleed to find the two founding races fighting between themselves, causing disunity for political and partisan reasons.
Hear, hear.
That is not so in this party.

Mr. Speaker, I believe in a democracy for this country. This is what all Canadians who are used to living in a democratic way believe in. They are used to having the opportunities presented by a democratic country. Opportunity is the dearest thing democracy gives to the people-opportunity to work, opportunity to realize ambitions, opportunity to voice opinions. But this is what the present government is trying to take away from the people of this country. This government has set its course and has said that the people of the country shall have what the government gives them. It is all very well to say that if any legislation which is passed is found to be detrimental to certain areas of the country the government which initiated that legislation, if it is still in office, or an ensuing government, can change the legislation so that the people receive equal benefits. But once a flag is approved it cannot be changed. And who takes the responsibility in this case?
Parliament.

Do 19 million Canadians take that responsibility? No. When the final vote is counted in this house, about 150 members of parliament, whipped into line in most cases, will say to the Canadian people: "This is the flag the Prime Minister told us to vote for. This is the flag we voted for, and this is the flag you are going to have for all time".

No.

speechtext: It is too late.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. I think it is my duty to remind the hon. member who

Canadian Flag
has the floor that he should as much as possible bear in mind the amendment and the subamendment which are now before the house.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hear protests, but the part of the hon. member's speech which was heard by the Chair referred to the question of a plebiscite. I realize that the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) has to move to his subject, but I would ask him to keep in mind in due course the decision reached yesterday by the house.

Mr. Speaker, I always try to abide by your ruling. I have respect for any occupant of the chair in this House of Commons. But my conception of the situation is that the subamendment proposes that the people of Canada should have the opportunity to express their opinion on four distinct questions. My remarks up to this moment have been directed to that and I do not intend to stray away from it. If you feel I am straying away from the subamendment at any time, please bring the fact to my attention; but up till now I beg to differ with Your Honour, even though I respect your decision. I still think I am keeping within the subamendment now before the house.
I suggest that other vital matters which have come before the people of this country, matters not so much in the federal field of jurisdiction because the opportunity has not presented itself in the federal field, but matters within provincial areas of jurisdiction and municipal areas of jurisdiction, have not been settled by the bodies governing those areas but by referendums which have been submitted to the people. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, if we continue on this path- and I believe this with all my heart-we will cause more disunity in this country than we have ever seen before, and we will never be able to heal it. I appeal to the government. It is not too late now. I speak with all sincerity when I say, give the people of this country the opportunity to say what they want.
The subamendment provides four choices. Those who wish to retain the red ensign will have the opportunity by secret ballot to indicate their feeling. Those who want modification of the red ensign can by secret ballot say so. Those who want the three maple leaves flag can so indicate by secret ballot. Those who want the one maple leaf design can also speak. And we know from

experience over the years that the people of this country will abide by the majority decision.
We are divided in this house, Mr. Speaker, and we are divided over this subamendment. There are those in the house who feel that the red ensign should be retained because it has served this country for so many years. Children have been born under it and immigrants have come here and found freedom under it. I speak as one whose parents came to this country at the ages of 17 and 16. They married here without a friend. Why did they come to Canada, Mr. Speaker? They came here to find freedom of opportunity, justice and liberty, things they never enjoyed in the country from whence they came. Because that flag gave them that opportunity, they worked hard. The opportunity was there and they were able to make a living in this country. They were able to set the foundation for people like myself to participate in the active life of this country, and they were, as I am, good Canadians. Surely those who would like to see modifications of the red ensign have a desire to give a prominent place to the two founding races.
I tome from people who believe in tradition and who do not throw tradition out the window when it has served its usefulness. I come from people who do not discard tradition in order to appease. I think it is good tradition that will not allow people to throw their parents out the door when they become too old. People have a responsibility to look after those parents. All of these things are part and parcel of human nature and upbringing.
We also have the proposal for the three maple leaf flag by the Prime Minister and the government. Surely those people who want to support it should have the opportunity of doing so by secret ballot, because here in this house we find the government as well as some other hon. members supporting this proposal. We also have a group of members in this house who feel that the one maple leaf flag is the flag that should be adopted for Canada. Mr. Speaker, we are divided in this house on this vital issue. I submit the country is being divided, and is perhaps even now divided. Many people have very strong feelings about this issue and unless we give them an opportunity to express those feelings by secret ballot, and experience the satisfaction that they have had a voice, we will never heal the wounds that will be inflicted upon this nation. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this

is the only way we can remove the flag issue from partisan politics.
Most of us have our constituents and their votes in mind when we vote on issues in this house. Let us take this issue out of partisan politics. I appeal to the Prime Minister to play no favourite with anyone, and let the people of this country decide this issue. All of us in this house have politics in mind during the debate on any issue, because we are all here as politicians. Most of the members in this house conduct polls in their ridings to find out the feeling of the majority of the people. Is that the procedure we are going to follow in deciding how to vote on this issue? Certainly that is the procedure most members will follow. I am sure every member representing a French Canadian riding will follow that procedure and vote in favour of the three maple leaf design because that is the will of the majority of the people in Quebec. What consideration is being given to the feelings of the people of Ontario? How are we going to heal the wounds that will be inflicted on half the people in a riding because they are divided evenly on this issue? Should one follow the wishes expressed by one half of the people in the hope that the remainder will forget about the situation? Certainly those people will not forget.
Mr. Speaker, I again urge the Prime Minister and the government to take this issue out of the arena of political partisanship in which we have found ourselves embroiled. Perhaps to do so will necessitate the spending of more money. Surely we are spending money in this country for various other reasons probably not as important as this. In my opinion this whole issue is one of the most important to come before this house since I became a member in 1952.
Let us consider for a moment the effect of the adoption of a new flag on the unity of this country. Do the Prime Minister and the government think that the adoption of the three maple leaf flag will bring unity to this country? That thought is far from the truth, Mr. Speaker.
As I said earlier, I am not of British origin, but I have often looked at British people and marvelled at the tolerance they have displayed. I do not know what would happen in another country if a symbol of the people's heritage was removed from the flag. I am not sure that there would not be a revolution. People's hearts must bleed when they witness that happening. Who is going to take down the flag which has stood in this country for so many years as a symbol to
Canadian Flag
the people who came and built this country and provided the opportunity to those of other races to come here and enjoy the liberty provided under this flag? Surely their hearts will bleed as a result of the adoption of the proposal of the government.
In view of human nature one cannot expect to take away something which is dear to the people's hearts, throw it out the window and have unity. Unity will never be created in this country if we follow that course, and I appeal to the Prime Minister and the government to abandon this mad policy. Give the people of this country an opportunity to speak silently one by one. I am sure they will make a choice and they will all agree with the choice of the majority. I am certain these people will not agree with a decision made by 150 or 160 members in this house, which is rammed down their throats. Those members will have to say they combined to adopt this flag for Canada and the people must accept it whether they like it or not. They must say to the people, this is your flag and no one can amend it.
Mr. Speaker, I think we must pursue a solution to this problem with a little more sanity. I think the government must reconsider its position and should not be adamant in its stand. Let us consider how the three maple leaf design was introduced. Let us consider the tortuous path its introduction travelled. The first unveiling of this three maple leaf design was carried out by the Prime Minister before a group of newspapermen in his own home. Even the cabinet was not aware of this design.
Order.
Even the caucus did not know about the design. In fact, no one knew about it other than the Prime Minister, and he wanted to observe the reaction to it and called the members of the press-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point
of order.
Do you have a point of order or a question of privilege, not that it really makes much difference?
This is just an excuse.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, irrespective of the remarks just made, my rising on a point of order to obtain the ruling of Mr. Speaker is not an excuse. A decision was rendered yesterday afternoon, and I think the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) has now

Canadian Flag
turned exclusively to a discussion of the main resolution before this house. That decision indicated clearly that a debate on a subamendment must be limited to the subject of the subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, the solicitude of the Minister of Justice does not command very much support. He stood silent when his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) was speaking. Surely we have not come to an occasion in this House of Commons when every time the Minister of Justice feels that anything said on this side contravenes the rules, as he would interpret them, he has to be listened to. Why was he so silent? Why did he sit so inert when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking?
Sir, the hon. gentleman who was speaking may not be speaking in a way that appeals to the sentiments of hon. gentlemen opposite, but if ever there was an hon. gentleman speaking with authority of heart and experience, it is the hon. gentleman for Ontario (Mr. Starr).

Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Minister of Justice has intervened in what I have said, but certainly I am not going into the history of both parties, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) did. I am staying entirely within a discussion of the subamendment, and have referred to the flags that subamendment has proposed as choices for the people of this country. I referred to the tortuous steps that were taken to introduce the new flag in an attempt to obliterate all tradition of this country. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce describes as appeasement the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) to have a fleur-de-lis on the red ensign, in an attempt to give the prominence to the founding races of this country which is their due, that is improper description. I have not endeavoured to go into the whole tortuous speech that he made.
And false, too.

He said that this was a gratuitous piece of appeasement in order to satisfy the French founding race of this country. After the unveiling to selected members of the press gallery the Prime Minister, without consulting his cabinet, without consulting the caucus or parliament, unveiled this flag before the Canadian Legion at their convention in Winnipeg. Only then did he go to the cabinet and ask for approval.

These are the steps taken. After that he came to the Liberal caucus and got their approval. Then he came to parliament. Meanwhile, sir, what was happening? Pins were appearing all over this country and being sold over the counter, on which there was the three maple leaf design, before parliament had an opportunity of discussing it. There were bathing suits in this design, too; they looked a lot nicer. The proposed design for a Canadian flag is now being put to commercial use. Is this the way in which a flag design for this country should be treated? We have bumper stickers, flags put on twigs and flown upside down to be used by reporters for the purpose of pictures, as happened last Saturday to the Leader of the Opposition and me. This is being foisted upon the people, and I think it is wrong. I think the people are beginning to resent this procedure.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister and his government to reconsider their position. This emblem that has been proposed by the Prime Minister is being used for every other purpose except a flag. The Minister without Portfolio has ordered 100,000 bumper stickers. [Translation]

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.
I did not place an order for 100,000 bumper strips, as stated by the hon. member for Ontario. However, I know that so many people are asking for them throughout Canada that 100,000 would be far from enough to meet the demand.
There is no point of order. [Text]

I was absolutely right, the Minister without Portfolio has ordered 100,000 bumper stickers. This is the purpose for which this proposed emblem is being used, even before it has been hoisted on a flagpole to be respected by the people of this country. This design is being made up in bathing suits, bumper stickers, and boloney is being sold under this insignia. Is this the sort of emblem of which we, as Canadians, can be proud? All of these stickers are being made, boloney, beer and all the other products are being sold under this insignia. This is what we are being asked to adopt as a flag. Everything else that has stood for our flag in the past is being dumped out of the window.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order. I suggest that it is up to the hon. member for Ontario to show that the type of discussion he is giving us now has anything to do with

the question of whether or not the questionnaire should read a certain way, as the hon. member for Regina City has suggested in his subamendment.

There are four choices listed in this subamendment, and I am discussing each and every one of them. I am discussing how they came about. I am saying that the red ensign has been our flag for years. Sacrifices have been made under it, freedom and opportunity have been found under it. I am discussing also how the three maple leaf flag has been brought about; that is all I am doing. These four questions are in the subamendment.
