speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I speak to the point of order? Before you entered the chamber this afternoon, sir, the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking. He dealt with the general subject of what he called the filibuster, gave us a lecture on that and made a personal attack on the Leader of the Opposition.
In his absence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
He discussed the Conservative party, its present position and its future. He then made a reference to the Leader of the Opposition and his address on a television program last week. He drew attention to the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition that some symbol of French Canada might appear on our flag. These were some of the subjects he discussed without interruption by the Speaker. It was a wide open debate. We ought not now to be denied a similar wide open debate just because the Minister of Justice is attempting to intervene.
There was no interruption from this side of the house. I suggest to you that reference should be made to Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 110. At the bottom of the page you will read this:
Freedom of speech is a sacred principle and if there is a place where it should be fully respected that place is the parliament of the nation, and it is
Canadian Flag
the Speaker's responsibility to see that this principle is not infringed upon.
The Minister of Justice is attempting to infringe upon the freedom of speech of the hon. member for Ontario when it was allowed, without interruption, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I suggest to you, sir, that the member for Ontario should be permitted to speak with the utmost freedom on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, on this issue our party does not intend to follow the partisan attitude and the political tones that have been injected into this flag issue by the Prime Minister and the government. I say that, sir, in view of what has been said by the Prime Minister. He has taken away the opportunity of the members of his party to vote according to their conscience. They must follow the line of the government on this question. He has stated his government will stand or fall on this issue, and that makes it a political issue. We do not intend to follow that line in this party. We believe this is a highly emotional issue and that the people of Canada should have an opportunity to voice their opinion by means of a referendum. There should be a vote by secret ballot in this country. I say this procedure will bring satisfaction to the people of Canada because they will have had an opportunity, as they have in the past, to decide the matter by a vote of the majority. It will bring unity to this country. We will have a country of which we can be proud, with a flag that will be chosen by the people themselves and not by politicians in this House of Commons who must knuckle under the whip of the party.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the privilege to rise in the flag debate at this time and to be the first to congratulate the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) who made such an eloquent speech in defence of democracy. I must reiterate his words in reference to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). I was amazed and discouraged to see a minister holding such an honourable position making such a partisan, prejudiced speech as he did in reference to the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and in reference to their right to get up in this house and speak in the interests of Canada's very distinctive national flag.
I want to support unequivocally the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) to the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and also to support the subamendment

Canadian Flag
proposed on Thursday last by my colleague, the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More). In my opening remarks I want to say that the undemocratic principle injected into the flag issue by the Prime Minister, in the manner in which he introduced the matter into the house, means that the Prime Minister has sown a wind and he will reap a whirlwind. I can substantiate that statement by an article which appeared lately in the press, referring to the plebiscite or referendum, an article by that well known and eminent writer, Patrick Nicholson, under date of August 12. He said:
The campaign strategists of the Liberal party have been halted in their tracks-stunned.
As most, but not all, Canadians know very well, parliament has long been stalled in its work largely because of "the flag issue." As the majority, but by no means all, of Canadians are uneasily conscious, this is dividing the country even more disastrously than the stormiest issue recorded in our history books-
He goes on to state what a recent poll showed:
It quickly became obvious that "Mike's maple" had attracted overwhelming support among French Canadians, while the lukewarm enthusiasm for it elsewhere was gravely tempered by the resentment, as some M.P.'s have expressed it, that this was "yet another concession to French Canada."
The lopsidedness of cross Canada sentiment on the flag issue has just been revealed by a nationwide poll, whose sensational results were given front page columns in Ottawa's thoughtful French language newspaper, Le Droit
The poll discovered that a majority of Canadians, in every province except Quebec, prefer the Canadian ensign to the maple leaf design. It also ascertained that about one third of all Canadians would prefer some other flag, such as the union jack or another design, or were ignorant or indifferent about the whole issue.
I do not want to be called to order on this, Mr. Speaker, and so I would like to point out that it refers to the subject of the subamendment in that it deals with whether we should have a maple leaf or a compromise on the red ensign. He goes on to say in this article:
The significance of these figures, in the eyes of all Liberal strategists thinking in terms of an election, is that they clearly show that the flag issue would bring disastrous Liberal losses in nine provinces, and leave that party largely as the political arm of French Canada.
This is a salient point. As the hon. member for Ontario so eloquently put it, we do not want to have an issue which, when developed and brought to a conclusion, will divide our country and bring disunity to this great nation, something that will take several generations to heal. Therefore it is evident to most Canadians and to us here in this house that we should take the advice of the Leader of the Opposition and have a plebiscite on

this matter to give Canadians a chance to look at it on a compromise basis, and decide in the quiet of their own hearts what should be a flag for Canada.
Many Canadians today are asking a number of questions which I think should be answered by the various members sitting opposite. I was very glad this afternoon to see at last a member of the cabinet get up in his place and speak, after having been silent so long, but let us hear from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidick-son). Let us hear from the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn), from the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey), from the hon. member for Hastings South (Mr. Temple), from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), from the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd), and from many others opposite who have sat silent. Let them answer some of these questions.
Why did the Prime Minister decide to bring the flag issue on to the Canadian political scene at this time? It was not in the throne speech.
Why does he not allow a free vote in parliament at this time?
Why does he want to hold the threat of an election over the heads of Canadians?
Why does he want to place this issue ahead of other more important pieces of legislation facing this parliament?
Why does he want to add this most divisive issue to the already over-charged political scene?
Why is he not striving for unity in Canada rather than sowing seeds of disunity?
Why is he taking the advice of the wrong people in these questionable decisions?
Why is he relegating what was once a great Canadian political party into a petty, selfish, partisan group representing only the political arm of French Canada?
Why does the Prime Minister want to take the Christian symbols off our flag?
Why does he jeoparidize the political wellbeing of so many of his own party members?
Why this all or nothing stand of the Prime Minister?
Why does the Prime Minister want to bury the past?
Why does the Prime Minister not want to set up a committee of both houses of parliament, as Mr. King did in 1945, to come to an agreement on this issue? Why? Why? Why?

These and many more questions are being asked by the people of our great nation.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, and people outside Canada also are asking these questions too, and this is causing me a lot of worry. When the peoples of the outside world look through the window and find us divided in our parliament over this contentious issue they ask the same questions, and the only person who is getting any satisfaction out of it is Mr. Khrushchev himself.
Let us take a look at what some of our people are saying about the plebiscite or referendum, and I think we would do well to take a look at outside opinion as well as expressing our own viewpoints in this house. In deciding to rise in this debate and give my own personal viewpoint I also want to give the viewpoints of the constituency I represent.
Last fall, prior to this debate being introduced, I sent a questionnaire to the people of my riding, a questionnaire which had five questions on it, the first being, "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign or a change?" In order to get a cross section of opinion I did not write just to my executive committee or my own personal friends. I directed the questionnaire to the reeves and councillors of the 25 municipal governments that lie within the boundaries of my riding, some 150 people in number, 25 municipalities, each with six councillors and an elected reeve. I felt these people would represent the opinion of the people of that area very well. Among other questions, one was, "Are you in favour of unemployment insurance for farm labourers?" Another was: "Are you in favour of lotteries?" But the first question was on the flag, and without exception the replies I received said they were in favour of the red ensign or a modification of it. To me this indicates that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition is right in asking that this issue be decided by the people of Canada through means of a referendum. I think, also, that my hon. friend from Regina City (Mr. More) was right in putting forward this subamendment specifying certain alternatives so that everybody might have the democratic privilege of making a decision on this issue.
Many hon. members have referred to the position taken by the Royal Canadian Legion, among them the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) in his eloquent address the other day. I think the voice of the Royal Canadian Legion, of the Canadian corps association, of the Orange Lodge of
Canadian Flag
British America and of other organizations of this character should be given full consideration. I might add that the British Israel world federation has produced a pamphlet about the flag setting out its origin, its symbolism and its significance. I would recommend this publication to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) who spent so much time in his amateur endeavours in heraldry before coming up with the maple leaf flag. I suggest that if he has not studied this pamphlet he might do so, because what is set out here is well worth reading. The heraldry and traditions of the red ensign are given, as well as the origins of the union jack, and so on.
I should like now to read into the record some comments regarding a plebiscite by Mr. Heesaker, dominion president of the Canadian corps association. He says:
The comments of our Prime Minister that those who support the retention of the Canadian red ensign are endeavouring to pressure the government into an election, have been made by him to simply confuse the flag issue. It is not the supporters of the present Canadian national flag who have been pushing this flag issue to the priority decision position that it has at this date reached in parliament, but it is the Prime Minister's personal endeavour to place his flag design on the flag poles of this country that has resulted in this issue reaching such controversial prominence. With such divided opinion through Canada on the flag question, we cannot understand why Mr. Pearson will not allow the people of Canada the opportunity to choose between the Canadian red ensign and his new suggested maple leaf choice.
We feel the supporters of the Canadian red ensign are more democratic in their viewpoint than the supporters of the maple leaf design for they are willing for this question to be submitted in referendum form to the people of Canada and to abide by their decision, where the maple leaf flag supporters are reluctant to trust the approval of their proposed new flag to the people of Canada! We do not wish to see our government waste money either, for it is the people of Canada who supply the money. The flag question ballot could be placed in with the regular voting ballots in the next scheduled general election of this country, and there most certainly is no need of either an election to be called, nor a ten million dollar immediate referendum when the question can be placed before the voters of this country when the next regular general election is scheduled, and in the meantime, the present national flag should be flown as it has been for the past many years until the people of Canada signify to the contrary.
Our organization fully realizes that there are many important national problems before the present members of the House of Commons that should most definitely take precedence over the flag question, and again we reiterate, that it is not the supporters of the retention of the Canadian red ensign as Canada's national flag, who are forcing this issue to the foreground in parliament.
It goes on to say:
In conclusion, I would like to mention that for the past half a century or more this country's prime

Canadian Flag
ministers and members of parliament have always indicated that Canada's veterans' views were respected statements by citizens who had served their country well in war, and were continuing to serve it loyally in peace through the welfare and service work of their organizations. During the past few weeks because of our present Prime Minister's open combat attitude against the veterans organizations views on the flag question, politicians, newspapers and general citizens, have openly ridiculed the ex-servicemen, who down through the years since 1900 have served Canada both home and abroad. This type of criticism by those particularly in government authority has damaged the prestige and character of "service organizations" and we trust that it was never the intention of our present government to do so.
There are others, in addition to the organizations I have mentioned, which support the red ensign and which have made strong pleas for a referendum. Here is a copy of an open letter to the Prime Minister. It states:
Please endorse red ensign which is my flag as third generation Canadian.
Our union jack symbolizes freedom without licence, equity without denial of personal rights to free men under it. Appeasement of minorities unjustly penalizes majority, and fatal to tolerant unity.
Here is a lady writing from Winnipeg, Manitoba. She puts her plea in the form of a little poem, and I think it would be timely to place it on record, too:
The Ensign
This is the flag for which men died In bloody, and ugly, and nightmare battle,
This is the flag!
This is the flag which death-bound rattle of guns Could never still,
This is the flag!
And now they fling its tatters to the waves,
And cry with glee, and trample underfoot Bright honour's face,
0	Canada, O Canada	
1	weep for all our race!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but he did indicate a moment ago that he would be referring to messages and a poem which, he said, had relevance to a referendum and to the red ensign. I heard no reference at all in those citations to anything having to do with a referendum or a plebiscite and in the circumstances it is my duty to remind the hon. member of the decision of the house yesterday.
While I am quite prepared to give the hon. member all possible latitude, I feel his remarks should be confined at this stage to the specific point which is now before the house.

Thank you. I can assure Your Honour I do not wish to depart very far from the rules of relevancy. But since

other hon. members have been allowed a certain flexibility I thought I was sufficiently in order.
To revert to the subamendment, it is my belief, as I have stated earlier, that this matter should be placed before the people of Canada, now that it has given rise to such widespread controversy. I feel, as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) said so eloquently, that the people should have an opportunity at some time in the future to go into a booth and mark an "x" opposite the flag of their choice. If this were done, we would never be faced with the accusation that the steps we are now taking are undemocratic and that such an important issue was being decided on a political basis. At this time in our history we should demonstrate to the people of Canada and to the world in general that we are democratic in our principles and that we solve our problems through democratic procedures. We on this side of the house should not be accused of filibustering at this time. We feel very deeply on this issue, which is one which goes to the hearts of our members. It is an emotional issue, not an economic one. If the Prime Minister would take this opportunity, which has been given to him by the Leader of the Opposition, to adopt a plebiscite, using the provisions outlined in the subamendment as a guide, I am sure we could settle this question without further controversy. I am confident this is the way in which the people of Canada feel it should be settled.
In closing my remarks I should like to say that I am definitely in favour of the retention of the red ensign. I say this on my own behalf and on behalf of my constituents, and I believe I am speaking also for most of the members of my party. I believe they would be agreeable to the compromise solution outlined by the hon. member for Regina City, and once more I should like to reiterate what others have said before me, namely that any country which dissociates itself from the past will have a questionable future.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a
question of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam) ?
Would the hon. member allow a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. Two members have risen at the same time. I believe the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) is asking permission to put a

question to the hon. member for Moose Mountain, if he wishes to answer.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has advocated this process of referendum in the selection of a flag. Would he be good enough to indicate to the house what countries have selected flags in this fashion?

I would like to answer that question by asking another question. I would like to ask the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) what country has disposed of its flag by the method now being taken by this government?
Hear, hear.
Is the hon. member trying to imply that he does not want a flag by proposing that the referendum be held at the next general election?

Mr. Speaker, before entering into this debate with regard to the subamendment I wish to also voice my approval of what was said by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). I offer my congratulations to the hon. member, who so ably expressed my personal opinions and I am sure expressed the feeling of everyone in the party to which I have the honour to belong. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we are now engaged in what is a most unnecessary and a most critical debate. It is unnecessary because the question should never have come before parliament; it is most critical because it is causing serious emotional complications throughout Canada, it threatens to divide our country beyond repair, and it is bringing discredit to the House of Commons at the present time.
We in parliament are spending time on an issue with regard to which the Canadian people wish to express their individual opinions. The answer is obvious in the subamendment, that Canadians must never be forced to accept a flag design contrary to the wishes of the majority; and it is their democratic right to be allowed to express their opinion. I offer no apologies for being somewhat repetitious. Repetition to correct an injustice is always justifiable.
Hear, hear.

All Canadians ask is for
justice, and for this flag resolution to be railroaded through is not justice. We want justice with a purpose and we want justice without partisanship. A lot more important things
Canadian Flag
could be done in the House of Commons at the present time than arguing about this flag issue. In my opinion the flag issue should never have come before the House of Commons. We see, in an editorial which appeared in the last night's Journal what people think of this debate. I believe this is a particularly important editorial and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I will read it in part:
Any flag that Mr. Pearson might ram through in these circumstances would serve as a symbol of division rather than unity.
How true that is:
Canada cannot afford that.
And as to legislation-the cost of Mr. Pearson's clinging to his course is indefinite postponement of the following business-
Then the editorial cites eight important bills that are before the house at the present time and are being sidetracked while we continue in the house, on this divisive flag issue, trying to obtain justice for the people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

I was interested in the hon. member's statement that he agreed with everything the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) had said. As I recall it, the hon. member for Ontario stated that this is the most important thing to face parliament since he has been a member. I wonder how the hon. member reconciles that statement with what he is now saying.

The answer to that question is obvious, Mr. Speaker. This important debate has been created because of the fact that the people of Canada insist on having a voice in what is going on in this house, and this is being denied by the government.
Hear, hear.

Canadian Flag
with experience. Where do we find experience in this issue? History relates experience. Can we learn through history; can we learn to avoid mistakes by the study of history? I claim that we can, and we should and we must. Canada insists on going from crisis to crisis. If we are not in an international crisis, if we are not in an international war, we create a crisis among ourselves. It seems to me that the crises we create in our own country, crises of our own making, mean we are happiest when we are in a turmoil.
The flag resolution of the government is causing great and deep bitterness, not only in parliament but particularly throughout this country. It is the greatest crisis since the first world war. This is where we get back into history. I would say it is probably the greatest internal crisis since confederation. I can recall, as I am sure other members of this house can, that one of the greatest crises we had in Canada was in 1911 when the reciprocity treaty was being brought into this house. How did they settle that question? The issue was so serious that it was dividing the east from the west-western Canadians wanted reciprocity; eastern Canadians did not want reciprocity. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in his wisdom, said, "This is a question for the people". He went to the people. Reciprocity was defeated; but everyone in Canada was satisfied-and they were satisfied because a plebiscite had been held.
Let us come down to 1917. This is another point in history. In 1917 we were at war. Conscription was considered unnecessary. The government of the time did not think they would have a plebiscite for conscription; they thought they would enforce it. This was in spite of the protests of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who said this was an issue that should be sent to the people. Mr. Speaker, all of us in this house know that the fact this issue was not sent to the people was one of the biggest mistakes made in Canada. It created division in our country, division so great that it has taken a whole generation to clear it up.
Now let me come to 1944 when we had a similar situation. Canada was at war. However, precedents offered guidance. The government of the day, under the leadership of Mr. Mackenzie King, realized that the conscription issue was something which would divide our country and asked for a plebiscite on the question. In spite of the urgency of wartime we took time to hold a plebiscite. Naturally some people were not satisfied with the result, but in general there

was no resentment and it kept the country from being divided.
Those were times of war, Mr. Speaker. Today there is no war; at least, there is no war as far as this country is concerned. There is no urgency to this matter. We have had the present flag for at least 40 years and it has been our official flag since 1945. Why do we have to rush into this question and decide it now when during the course of our previous history it has been shown on several occasions that on an issue of this type only a plebiscite can clear the matter up? This issue today, if it is not dealt with by means of a plebiscite, promises to create the greatest cleavage Canada has ever seen, and I say that knowing the sentiments of the people throughout the country, having spoken with them from coast to coast. This crisis is the result of an ill-conceived step on the part of the government. The flag issue has become political when it should be outside party politics. The government should never have forced a particular design of flag on the country and said: Either the flag is accepted or we will have an election. This matter is too serious to treat lightly, in a "take it or else" fashion. This is something which must be discussed. It is not a question which is going to affect us only today; it will affect our country for generations to come. We want our children, our grandchildren and our great grandchildren to say that we have a beautiful flag. Therefore we must be careful to give them a flag which will make them proud to be Canadians. This flag issue, if properly handled, can solve the problem of national unity, there is no doubt about that. If it is handled properly our national unity will be stronger than it has ever been in the past. A national referendum, as suggested in the subamendment, will overcome any resentment. The people must decide this issue, Mr. Speaker.
At this time I could go into the history of the red ensign but I realize that I would probably be speaking outside the terms of the subamendment. Suffice it to say that the red ensign has represented the united life of our country. It has represented Canada in peace, in war, in commerce. It is the emblem of our nation and is recognized throughout the world. It also indicates the design of Canadian history. It shows our association with that great organization, the British commonwealth of nations. It has a glorious history. The history of how it came about is, of course, well known to this house; but let

me briefly say this. The three Christian crosses of St. George, St. Patrick and St. Andrew are part of our tradition and history. We just do not eliminate such things easily. We must not allow ourselves to discard all our traditions. The shield is of course traditional. It represents parts of Canada and denotes the great history of our founding races in generations past, and I hope for generations to come.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, why is it necessary under these circumstances to eliminate the union jack from our flag, whatever may be the design decided upon? That question has never been answered. Why is it necessary to have a second flag and call it the union jack? Has any other country in the world two flags? I do not know of one. I do not see why we should have two flags. Is one flag to be flown in one part of Canada and a second to be flown in the second part of the country? Would that be in the best interests of a united Canada? Would it not differentiate between parts of Canada and create a more serious division? I say, let us deal with this subject by creating unity, not division, in our country.
Some people complain about our present ensign because its design is similar to the British merchant marine flag. But what more honourable organization could it resemble? The British merchant marine has been the organization which has kept alive the British commonwealth. It has done more for the progress of the world than any other organization. Why should we not be proud to belong to, and be associated in our emblems with, that great commonwealth of nations?
On the other hand, a design has been proposed which this house is asked to accept, they say without argument. This design represents the merchant marine of another nation, a nation not particularly friendly to this country. Why should we accept their design and discard one with such tradition and connections with the commonwealth of British peoples? Many flags of different countries resemble each other. Sometimes when travelling around Europe one must almost take out the geography book to see which flag he is looking at. There may be a little variation here and there, with the same colours being changed around in different ways. But there is nothing wrong in having a flag which resembles another flag. These are all petty criticisms and are ineffective.
The red ensign has been accepted as Canada's flag. It is known throughout the world as Canada's flag. People throughout the world 20220-441
Canadian Flag
do not know what we are talking about when we say we want a new flag. How long would it take Canada to produce another flag which would be recognized throughout the world as such, as the Canadian red ensign is now so recognized? The question is, Mr. Speaker, where are we going from here? What do we mean by a distinctive flag? In my opinion a distinctive flag is one which we can recognize as Canadian, wn.ch will be recognized throughout the world as Canadian, one which will be approved by Canadians, is acceptable to Canadians, and will unite Canadians. That is what the subamendment wants to bring about, and it is exactly what we are after. The people wish to have a voice in the choice of a flag. The people want to indicate which flag should be adopted. A referendum will not only give us an indication of their choice but create unity, which I believe is very important.
It is not a dereliction of the duty of the members of this House of Commons to suggest that this issue should be referred to the people. I think this suggestion indicates we have confidence in the people of our country to choose that with which they will be satisfied. A decision to adopt a flag without a referendum I believe is an insult to the intelligence of the people of this country who wish to express their opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think or believe that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was correct when he stated that under the British system of principles a plebiscite was a negation of the existence of parliament?
I am sorry, I did not understand the last part of the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the member feel the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was correct when he argued that under the British system a reference to a plebiscite was the very negation of the existence of parliament?

Mr. Speaker, I am not certain what the hon. minister is referring to, but I should like to state that the history of our country would indicate, as evidenced by the several examples I cited, that a referendum is the answer to this kind of issue.

You do not agree with your leader.

Canadian Flag
I do not question my leader's statement at all, but I do suggest the issue he may have been discussing was probably something entirely different from and unrelated to this type of issue.
He was referring to conscription.

I am not sure what the issue is you are referring to and therefore cannot discuss it more thoroughly.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I believe the holding of a referendum would constitute a compliment to the people of Canada. The government has indicated that it obtained a mandate as a result of the last election and now has authority to bring in a new flag. In my opinion that suggestion is entirely wrong and I emphatically disagree with it. The members of the government party must remember that they formed a minority government and were elected by a minority vote in this country. They must also remember that very few voters knew there was a flag plank in their platform. In my opinion 99 per cent of the voting public did not realize there was a flag plank in the Liberal party's platform. The majority of people are amazed to now learn of the existence of that plank. I am sure had they known there was a flag issue, as some of them must have known, they were not aware of the proposed design. It is my belief there is not one man in this House of Commons today who had any idea about the proposed flag design. I do not agree with the suggestion that because the government obtained what it has referred to as a mandate from the people of this country, most of whom had not the slightest idea there was to be a new flag, nor of course of any proposed design, it should be allowed to force a flag upon the country. I think the suggestion that the government has obtained a mandate in respect of the flag issue is absolutely without foundation.
Mr. Speaker, I believe this flag issue and the new design proposed by the government could not have been placed before this parliament at a worse time. We have a splinter parliament and we are creating a splinter nation. We need a unified nation. We should not carry this debate to a point of creating an irreparable division of the country.
If there is a desire on the part of the people of this country to have a new flag perhaps we should go to the Indian citizens and ask them their preference. Those citizens have lived under our flag since we came to this country and took it from them. I have

not heard one Indian express a desire for a new flag.
There are millions of Europeans in this country. We have listened to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr). He is of European origin and has voiced the opinion of millions of citizens of other racial origins who have adopted Canada and its emblems, and fought for Canada under the red ensign. These people have not expressed complaints but are proud to be Canadians. I suggest it is extremely questionable that the majority of the people in Canada today wish to replace our present red ensign.
I am sure the people of Canada do not resent the maple leaf as one of our national emblems but rather are very proud of it. The people of Canada do resent being forced to accept something without being allowed to express an opinion. They resent arrogance of any kind but particularly when it is displayed in respect of a most serious issue of this kind.
Mr. Speaker, I am here in this chamber to represent my constituents. Some members of this house have suggested they are not here to represent their constituents but to express their own personal opinions. I repeat that I speak and work for my constituents and can say that the majority insist there be no change. I have received hundreds of letters asking me to oppose any change in the present flag.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit me to ask a question. He has said he is here to represent his constituents. Does he not think that under our parliamentary system he is properly here to represent all of Canada and not just his constituents?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to that question I should point out that it is absolutely obvious that my constituency is part of this country of Canada. My constituents are proud to live in a part of Canada and their voices must be heard in this country.
I have received a few letters representing the other side of the argument, and I have had the privilege on several occasions to talk with the people who wish to have a new flag. I have asked these individuals whether they favour the adoption of this proposed design but have yet to hear one answer in the affirmative. Most of them were surprised when I told them the proposed design was the one they must accept without the benefit of choice. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that a stroll down the main street of Kamloops is similar

to a trip through a hornets' nest. Everyone asks me what we are doing about the flag issue and suggests that we should retain the red ensign.
Many think that the letters we have received are the result of an organized propaganda campaign. I represent ten Canadian Legion establishments in my constituency and I know how the members feel about this issue. These people have a right to voice their opinions in this country. They have fought for this country and their suggestions should be given some consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that press polls are not always accurate, but they do indicate that the people of Canada are two to one in favour of the retention of the red ensign. I challenge every member from British Columbia-I am glad to see there are at least two here-to ask their constituents to see what they should do on this flag issue. I ask these same men to ask their leader for a free voice on this vote. I ask them to vote according to their conscience and according to the wishes of their constituents. If they do this, I have no doubt what the result will be on this particular issue. I know we will have a plebiscite.
I do not believe that the holding of a plebiscite means it is necessary to have an election. I believe that the holding of a plebiscite could await the next general election. There is no hurry about this. We have had this flag for many years. The plebiscite could await the next general election and in this way it would not cost us anything at all, just a ballot. Then a flag would be chosen which would be acceptable to all the people.
I am not trained in heraldry. I do not know anything about flag design. I have no training in art, but I appreciate a good picture when I see it. I have some feeling when I look at a flag. I want to look at a flag of which I can be proud. I want to be able to say, "I am a Canadian; that is our flag; is it not beautiful?" There must be a certain amount of colour balance in this thing; I think that is the way you describe it. It must not be insipid. It must not look like a piece of wallpaper. It must have something of which you can really be proud. It must have some history. It must be something to which we can look forward with enthusiasm.
My constituents are protesting. There is something lacking in this particular suggestion for a new flag. They want to retain the red ensign. I do not believe we are going 20220-441J
Canadian Flag
to create more division in our country if another design, including some symbols of our historic background, is available. If democracy is to be made to work, we must respect the wishes of the people. People must be allowed to express their opinions. These people who are so anxious to preserve our present flag should not be restricted. Minorities should be allowed to express their opinions the same as majorities. A plebiscite will appease their antagonism. It would prevent national disunity. A plebiscite, as suggested in the subamendment, will leave no doubt as to what we should do.
As I say, this has become an extremely emotional issue, and this is the most dangerous thing that can happen to our confederation. As I have said, there is no hurry for a decision on this matter. A referendum can be held at any time. This is not an election issue and never should have been-considered as an election issue. There should! never have been any mention of an election in connection with this issue. It should have been dealt with in a reasonable way and the people should have been allowed to choose what they wish. It should have been outside party politics. This matter has become a purely partisan one in this house and we should not allow it to further divide our country, or we will be in for serious trouble.
A vote for a referendum, as I have suggested, is a vote for freedom of choice. It is a vote for unity within confederation. It is a vote for democratic principles and it is not necessarily a vote against the proposed flag. Is the government so confident of its design, is it so confident it is right that it is afraid to let the people vote on the issue? If the government feels the public are in favour of this new flag, what could they be afraid of? What would a plebiscite change? If they are right and the people are in favour of this, as they say, what are they afraid of? I appeal to the members of this house to let us have a national flag and not a party flag.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

I shall be finished shortly, and then you can ask your question.
In closing, I should like to say this: I think that this plebiscite, as recommended in the subamendment, is the best thing for Canada at the present time. I say, let us unify ourselves as Canadians. Let us be a parliament with a purpose. Let us declare our wishes as Canadians, and let us accept the flag as

Canadian Flag
Canadians. Let us unify our country. Let us march forward under a flag of which we can be proud. Let us get back within the realm of sanity. Let us have leadership and not chaos. Let us support the subamendment in order to preserve the unity of our country and march forward under a flag of which the vast majority of Canadians can say, "I chose that flag."
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he know of a country which was given a flag through a plebiscite or referendum, whatever you call it?

This question was answered a few minutes ago. If the hon. member will tell me of a country that has changed its flag in the manner in which we are attempting to do here, then I will answer the question.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time simply to say that if my friends on the right will ever permit me to do so I will vote for their amendment, and for a plebiscite on the flag. I have been in favour of a plebiscite from the start of this flag debate since I believe it is a very fair and reasonable way of settling the issue. I have been waiting now for three weeks in order to vote for the Conservative amendment. I will vote for it just as soon as they allow me to do so.
In a few more days I have to leave to go to my constituency on important constituency business. I am afraid that the vote will be taken before I can return. I should like to get it on the record, if I may, that if the Conservatives would allow me to vote for their amendment, I would do so now. If I had a vote I would vote in favour of the amendment.
Question; let us vote.

Mr. Speaker, on an emotional subject such as the one we have been discussing it is the duty of a member of parliament to register his position. A number of things have been mentioned on the flag question and I make no apologies for repetition.
The subject is one which should not have been introduced for debate in this house but which should have been settled by a plebiscite. The question of whether or not we should vote on a Liberal party flag is one that should not be brought before the house. In western Canada the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) replied, "Oh, we had an election and the people voted for us. We had a flag

plank in our platform." The only time the Liberal candidate who ran against me mentioned the flag was when he hesitantly agreed with the Legion in his home town that the red ensign was the best flag for Canada. That was the last we heard of the flag issue from him.
We should be attending to some other business in this house, matters that should be brought in and discussed fully, not things that will be hauled away from the house before being decided. There are health and welfare matters that should be discussed. There are agricultural matters that should be discussed-
Order.

My hon. friends yell order but I would refer them to these words of the subamendment, "and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following", and I would point out that certain questions are listed and there are others that might be listed. One of the other things we could be talking about is agriculture, even though a recent issue of a western farm paper said there had not been much time spent on agriculture, mainly because the previous minister of agriculture had done so much that there was little left to do right away. These are some of the things we should be discussing rather than spending our time dividing the country on a very emotional issue.
If we are to have a flag agreeable to a majority of the people, how do we achieve it? You certainly do not achieve it the way the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has attempted to do so. You do not antagonize the people of Canada, and then force a flag on them. You do not divide the country and then force a flag on it. This is not the way to get a worth-while flag for the country. You do not take a flag and thrust it down the throats of the Canadian people.
When the Prime Minister first brought forward his flag proposal he had far more support for the maple leaves than he has now. The Liberals are losing support because of their arrogance and contempt for the people of Canada. How much better it would be to have a referendum and settle this question properly. Among the questions which the subamendment proposes is that of the red ensign and the modifications that might be made to it. Personally I am in favour of the red ensign with modifications, to show the heritage of our history. I am and will be

utterly and forever opposed to the three maple leaf foliage which, as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) pointed out, is no more than a carton trademark, something I personally would hesitate to fly at any time.
What are we going to have if we adopt this flag? We are going to have everybody in Canada flying their own flag. People will say, "Mr. Pearson can have his flag, and so can I." That is their attitude towards this subject, which has been bungled, and bungled badly by the government. I believe I speak for a majority of my constituents when I say we should have the red ensign with modifications to show our dual heritage. Such a flag would show something of the freedoms we have in Canada, freedoms we would like to preserve.
One of these freedoms is freedom of the press, which to all intents and purposes we have lost at the moment. We have newspapers like the Edmonton Journal coming out with large editorials dealing with the red ensign and the plebiscite-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. I have the impression that the hon. member is straying away from the subject before the house.
He is right on the dot.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. I feel he is straying away from the subject matter now before the house and, as he knows, there was a decision of the house rendered yesterday. I feel it is the duty of all hon. members to try to abide by the decision of the house, which was to the effect that hon. members taking part in the debate at this stage-
What about the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -including the Minister of Trade and Commerce, should limit themselves to the specific point at issue.

On that point, Mr. Speaker, I am trying to establish some of the reasons why I think the second question in the subamendment is the one I favour, and why I think it is an ideal solution as a plebiscite question. I see nothing out of the way in stating why I think the red ensign with modifications is a good idea to have as a question in a plebiscite.
I was mentioning that we were losing some of the freedoms we fought for over the years, and one of those freedoms which we have pretty nearly lost is freedom of the press. If Your Honour will allow me I would like
Canadian Flag
to point out two or three instances in this regard. The most blatant one is the recent dismissal from Maclean's of six editors because they would not follow the Liberal line, and there was not one pressman with enough gumption to stand up and defend his fellow journalists who were thrown out of their profession because they would not follow a flag with three maple leaves. Is this the kind of freedom we are going to have under these three maple leaves, which I would like to label as the pettiness, pomposity and petulance of the Prime Minister? The three maple leaves are going to take away our freedom. This is not the kind of flag I want to live under, nor the kind of flag my constituents want to live under.
I would like to mention that the managed press in Canada is kowtowing to the Liberal line. The Edmonton Journal had a long editorial in favour of the red ensign and a plebiscite, but it got the word shortly thereafter and it has been particularly quiet ever since. It published the results of its own referendum and in northern Alberta, an area which is basically Anglo-Saxon but which has a mixture of all nationalities and has a substantial number of our French Canadian friends, who are some of our best citizens, this area was 65 per cent in favour of the red ensign.
We need the union jack on our flag to preserve this very vital freedom, this freedom of the press which we are losing, if we have not already lost it to big business which controls the publishing industry. These people are trying to mould public opinion in favour of the foliage flag, in favour of pettiness, pomposity and petulance.
Would the hon. member permit a question? I was wondering if he was not aware that three maple leaves was the emblem of Canada selected under a Conservative administration?

The three
maple leaves were designed by a former king of England and I am surprised my Liberal friends would pick them up as a slogan for Canada. We in western Canada, if we do see maple leaves, certainly do not see three of them on one stem. I do not think it is a botanical possibility in any case. As I say, personally I have no use whatever for this foliage flag and I will never fly it in any place over which I have jurisdiction, wherever I may be. As I have said, this foliage flag means nothing. I can only say it is a product of petulance, pettiness and pomposity on the part of the Prime Min-

Canadian Flag
ister. It probably reflects more than anything else the attitude of this government to date. We have seen budgets come and go. We have seen 60 days of decision come and go. We are now in the midst of a flag debate, which will continue because it is of vital importance to the majority of the people of Canada.
This is not something which hon. members opposite can decide, because they believe they are almighty. They are not. They will have to answer to the people eventually. If they persist in trying to force this foliage flag through, and if they succeed, it will be known as a Liberal party flag. It will be a political flag and nothing more.
Passed by parliament.

Passed by parliament by trained seals following a leader. Have a free vote if you want to talk that way. Have a free vote, and I would like to see how some of the hon. members over there would vote, including the hon. lady.
What would happen on your side?

Don't worry
about our side. This three leaf flag will become a political flag-a flag which will go out on every piece of Liberal propaganda in the next election.
Oh, oh.

Of course it will, particularly in certain areas, because the Liberals believe in a policy of divide and conquer. This is a dictum of the Liberal party and it dates from the days of Mackenzie King: You cannot win the country politically if there is unity; you must have the west fighting the east and then you pick up the pieces and become the big cheese. This was Mackenzie King's dictum, way back; the only way to win political power was to divide and conquer, and we in the west suffered from that policy for many years.
I say to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) that if he and some of his hon. friends from Quebec were less interested in the question of provincial autonomy and more interested in Canada as a whole we would have more success in building up a greater country. He might also be helping the people of his province a great deal more than he has done in the past if he would think in broader terms and contemplate a wider horizon. We in western Canada have always
[Mr. Homer (Jasper-Edson) .1
been accused of being radicals, even on occasion of being separatists. But we believe in Canada and we are willing to make sacrifices in order to remain part of Canada. I want to see Canada grow. I do not think it can grow under this three maple leaf device. We believe it is much better to have the red ensign which means something to our people, and I am sure even those members in the back benches of the Liberal party must have been thrilled when the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), of neither Anglo-Saxon nor French origin, got up and made the speech he did this afternoon. It was an example of what Canada can and should be under a flag such as the red ensign, perhaps with modifications to show our dual heritage. In this way we could go ahead in unity. The only manner in which this could possibly be done now is by means of a plebiscite.
We did not force this flag issue on the House of Commons. It was brought on by the Prime Minister saying, in his petulance, that he must fulfil at some time at least one of the promises made during the election. So he pushed this issue before the house in an effort to force this flag down our throats, trying to force upon us an artistic monstrosity which does not mean anything and which the majority of Canadians do not want. It is not good enough for the hon. member to say "just vote on it".
On the plebiscite.

There are others on this side who want to speak. I was talking earlier about freedom of speech. This is something which may be unheard of in Liberal ranks. But we believe we should learn from history and we would like to have the red ensign continue as our flag. We believe in the freedom of speech and in the freedom of the press and we would like these things to continue. We have had an example in this very debate of what might happen if we did not enjoy freedom of speech. We would have a foliage flag forced down our throats without regard to the opinions of the people of Canada, which would be a most divisive thing and would spoil the heritage on which this nation is built. We need this plebiscite. I think all hon. members, particularly those in the back row over there, should sit down and re-examine their positions; indulge in a little self-hypnosis and come out in favour of the subamendment.
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I had said that if we go ahead and pass this foliage flag of three maple leaves, which I designated as representing the pettiness, the pomposity and the petulance of the Prime Minister, we would cause nothing but disunity in Canada. I would like to spend just a few minutes saying how a plebiscite of the nature outlined in the subamendment could foster unity in Canada and make it a better, greater and more prosperous nation. One of the most serious things that is besetting confederation at the moment is this unsettling idea of the disunity that has been fostered, particularly in the province of Quebec but also in my own province in western Canada. While not so much has been heard about it, there is in each of the areas of Canada, I am sure, that local pride, that local necessity to promote their own area which fosters regionalism and makes separatism feasible to the people in these areas. This is, after all, Canada's greatest problem at the moment.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister has done a disservice to Canada by bringing forth the flag issue at this particular time. There is no doubt about it, nobody asked for a new flag particularly. Why should we change our flag; this is the question. It is not a question of giving us a flag all of a sudden; we have had a flag for 100 years. Why should we have a new one right now, when we have all sorts of problems that are related to confederation, that are related to our being a vast country different in geographical areas, different in areas of ethnic origin, different in what people are doing, and different in economic potential. In the face of these problems, why should we suddenly try to give them one little symbol that is supposedly going to make them all happy? But, Mr. Speaker, it is not going to do that. Ordinary common sense tells us that this is going to be a divisive issue; that this is going to foster disunity, not unity. The only way we are going to get that on to the right track, the only way we can try to bring Canada to that kind of unity we would all like to see, whereby all peoples of all ethnic origins can live, work, prosper and develop together, is by having a majority vote on this very emotional question.
It is not good enough for a few cabinet ministers, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) this afternoon, to rise
Canadian Flag
and rant and rave about filibuster, and so on. This issue is far more important than that. I would have thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce would have had more knowledge of the people he is governing than he displayed this afternoon. We must have, if we are going to achieve unity, that area of co-operation that is necessary to do this. Whether you want to call it co-operative federalism, or not, does not matter; but we have to be one country.
I am sure the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) appreciates that you cannot go around stealing industries from one area and giving them incentives to settle in another, providing jobs in one area at the expense of another. This is the sort of thing that will also foster disunity, and it is already taking place to a certain degree. We need something that is going to bring us unity. We are not going to get it under this foliage flag. We are going to get it only if we have a plebiscite.
I think the idea of having four questions is a good one, because this will give people in all parts of Canada a chance to express their opinions and they want to express their opinions. The Liberal party did not fight the last election in most areas of Canada, on the question of the flag at all. As I said earlier my Liberal opponent mentioned it only once. He said he was in favour of the red ensign and then backed off this question for the rest of the campaign. This was pretty general in the rest of Canada. So to say now they have a mandate to bring in a new flag is just nonsense, because they do not have a mandate to bring in this kind of flag at all.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we need a plebiscite as a unifying force in this country, as a democratic way of settling a difference. Then the majority decision will be accepted by the people of this country. Along this line we need, in order to promote unity in Canada, the communications media orientated to Canada as a whole. We have had the C.B.C. and other communications media, notably the press, orientated mostly to promoting themselves and not at all to promoting Canada. They have been destructive instead of constructive. They have not promoted the idea that we should have one Canada and a single symbol for one Canada. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, a single symbol that will make Canada united is one that has an historic background; one that will give our dual heritage full play; one that is acceptable to the people who came here from other nations partly because the union jack was on the flag we are flying and its freedom was all they

Canadian Flag
wanted. This is the only reason many people came to Canada in the first place; I have been told this many times. People of our various ethnic groups want their chance to say now what kind of flag we are going to have.
There are the four questions that could be posed to them if a plebiscite were held. There is the question: Are you in favour of the red ensign? Are you in favour of the red ensign modified-as I am-to show our dual heritage? Are you in favour of the three maple leaves? If we can trust the newspaper polls-and I never trust anything that is printed in the newspapers any more, after having come to parliament-
Hear, hear.

-the majority of people in Canada in nine provinces do not want this foliage flag. That is, if you can trust anything that is printed in the newspapers, as I say. I do not; I am just putting that forward.
The other question is with regard to the single maple leaf. The only disadvantage I see to a single maple leaf is that it does not denote anything. I think the three maple leaves denote, as I have said, several characteristics of this government and of the Prime Minister, but the single maple leaf would not denote anything. It is not a national botanical specimen, and we in western Canada would rather have the beaver or even the buffalo. We think these are national emblems. Why do we not have a rose?
Or Diefenbaker.

We could do all right with that, too. Still the question remains that all of us have to think on a proper basis along more than strictly provincial lines. This is the serious challenge thrown out to all members of parliament. We must quit being regional in the sense that we must have a particular flower or leaf from our area to be used as a symbol. The easiest and most historic thing which will unify Canada is for us to have a red ensign modified to show our dual heritage.
I say let the people of Canada decide. Let the people vote on a plebiscite composed of these four questions. Surely the only other answer is for the government to allow a free vote amongst its backbenchers without any brainwashing. That is the only alternative to a plebiscite. If the Prime Minister will lose some of his pomposity and petulance, then we can get on with the business of Canada and settle the question of a symbol very

easily. Once we are prosperous and working together this can be done. To continue in this manner is to continue to divide the country, and confederation will be meaningless in the near future if the government persists in its pattern to date.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the constituents I represent in the historic county of Pictou I wish to take part in this debate, which itself is an historic one. I subscribe to the terms of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), and I shall be referring to it in my remarks more fully.
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) brought forward in his speech a few matters which he said pertained to the subamendment; and in view of the fact that he was permitted to carry on and bring forward various matters I think at this time I should be able to comment briefly on the points he raised. The minister said that the official opposition were carrying out a filibuster in this debate. As pointed out by my hon. friend the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) on another occasion, a filibuster means to impede the progress of legislation. In this case it means to impede the progress of the House of Commons and of parliament itself. That is not the interpretation which I place upon my speaking in this debate, Mr. Speaker, nor is it the interpretation of the official opposition or of many people in this country.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is on record as pointing out that the members of this house should speak in this debate and have the right to have their say. If hon. members opposite do not wish to do this, that is their business. But if we on this side do wish to do this, then that is democracy at its highest.
Several months ago one of the members sitting on the other side-I will not point him out-said to me when sitting down at the table one day: "What is the point of going on with the debate on the flag? You are going to lose the vote anyway. You might as well give up the ghost." Yesterday in this house, someone on the other side-it is recorded in Hansard as "An hon. member"- said "We will rub you off". This was said after the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) said names would be rubbed off monuments. If we, the official opposition, and the people of this country were to give up the ghost and cease to fight, then certainly nothing would be accomplished in the way it was accomplished during the period since confed-

eration in making this country of ours the great country it is. If the allies in the last war had given up when the Germans told them that they would defeat them, so what was the point of keeping on, where would we be today? They even sent a spy over to England to talk the U.K. and our allies into surrendering. I believe it is worth fighting a battle when principles are at stake in which you believe; and we certainly have principles on our side in this case.
The minister also said that the control of the business of the House of Commons is in the hands of the leaders who were meeting today. I took some notes of what he said, but as they are not verbatim I can be corrected. I might point out it was a different matter in 1962, when the government of that day was charged by the opposition with being in charge of the business of the house, rather than the various leaders of the parties. It is a different matter, now that hon. members opposite are on the government side. The official opposition were also accused of irresponsible manoeuvring. It seems to me that in this regard the irresponsibility should be placed at the doorstep of the Prime Minister and of the government for bringing forward this flag resolution and pressing it upon the people of Canada. Let us put irresponsibility where it belongs and look at this question in an objective manner.
Confederation in the spirit of Macdonald and Cartier was also mentioned. I think the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) got up and asked, where was the spirit of Macdonald and Cartier. Of course, the Minister of Trade and Commerce wondered about that, but said it is not present in this modern age. I suggest that in this debate the members of the government have no free vote. The minister said that parliament should decide the issue of the flag. I suggest that parliament is the proper body to look into this question and decide the issue if hon. members on both sides of the house are given a free vote and are able to vote as their conscience dictates. In the days of Macdonald and Cartier, when men from all over the country were brought together to form and to weld the nation which we have today, there was certainly no doubt as to a free vote. Those Fathers of Confederation became members of this house and of this parliament of Canada and they were free to do so. They were not pitched into it by any party. They showed their own independence, and we need more of that in this parliament today.
The minister said, among other things, let us not appease anybody. I am not going to go 20220-442
Canadian Flag
beyond the terms of the subamendment, but in speaking of appeasement let us not forget that there is another resolution to follow, that concerned with the adoption of the union jack. As has been said on a previous occasion, there are two flags-one for show by the government and one for Joe, the premier of Newfoundland.
The minister also said he has been disappointed by the speeches of opposition members. He said there was sincere evidence of spirit but none of tolerance and conciliation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: And he will be disappointed with yours, too.

The hon. member's greatest contribution to the house is to sit there and mumble. Sometimes he appears on Hansard and sometimes he does not; but in either case he makes no real contribution. I hope that he will speak later on. I always like to hear him speak and to read his speeches, because they can be used on other occasions.
With regard to the question of a free vote I thought I might look into the original stand taken by the Prime Minister and dwell on that for a few moments. First there was to be a free vote given to the members of the House of Commons. Other members have made this suggestion and I think it is worth repeating at this time.
There was a suggestion that any vote on the flag issue would be considered as a confidence vote and any defeat in respect of the Prime Minister's motion would be considered to be a defeat of the government. Following that suggestion, of course, the Prime Minister challenged the opposition to an election. This then became a political football.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) this afternoon read part of an editorial which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. This evening I should like to read from the May 21, 1964 edition of that newspaper. I do not intend to read this item completely, Mr. Speaker, but I feel portions of it should be repeated during this debate. The portion I wish to quote commences as follows:
The so-called "free" vote on the flag issue is so much double talk, a mere sham.
The article then continues:
It matters little that Mr. Pearson says that any member of the Liberal party voting against the design submitted by the government would not be read out of the party. To our mind, such assurance is meaningless, and is not characteristic of Mr. Pearson.

Canadian Flag
Another portion of the article states:
We do claim, however, that the Liberal members would not line up unanimously behind the government's choice of flag-as it appears they are going to do-if party loyalty and the government's future did not hang in the balance. It is impossible to believe, for example, that all the Liberal members from the Atlantic provinces-where sentiment in favour of the red ensign seems overwhelming- would vote contrary to the wishes of their constituents.
The article then indicates that the flag issue is different from other issues brought forward by the government. This issue has been brought forward as a political football. It involves a flag proposed by the Prime Minister, with the help and assistance of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), and will not give Canadians the opportunity of expressing their views. The Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that parliament should decide this issue. I would be in support of that statement if a free vote was held.
In reference to item 3 of the subamendment relating to the three maple leaf design, as other hon. members have pointed out, this does not represent a distinctive Canadian flag. Maple trees do grow in various parts of the United States and other countries and are certainly not distinctive to Canada. Mr. Speaker, I received an interesting letter in this regard, as did the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales), who quoted a portion of it, which appears in Hansard of July 3, 1964 at page 5019. I should like to repeat that quotation as follows:
If Canada should have a new flag ... it should at least have a definite Canadian identification and not maple leaves.
Mrs. Young of Avondale Station, one of my constituents sent me several samples of our maple leaves. Following your ruling last night, Mr. Speaker, in respect of the various flags produced by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) I decided not to bring the samples with me. I should like to read a portion of Mrs. Young's letter as follows:
Enclosed please find a few samples of our maple trees. So that you may have the evidence to show the Prime Minister that the red maple of Canada is not the one he plans to paint red on his flag. The Canadian red maple is rubrum, and the one shown on the flag designs we've seen, look more like the "Norway maple" which is an introduced tree, or the "sugar maple" which is Canadian and American but not red in colour. It turns yellow in autumn.
We think the Prime Minister and others should be better acquainted with our beautiful red maple whose leaves are distinctive but not like the Norway maple.

The suggestion is that the proposed design with the three maple leaves is not representative of a maple leaf distinctive to Canada. Undoubtedly the hon. member for Leeds dealt fully with this matter, and he will correct me if I am wrong when I say that the evidence indicates that the proposed maple leaf on the flag design is not distinctive to Canada.
I should like to read from an article written by Mr. Roland Sherwood, which appeared in the Pictou Advocate of June 4, 1964 with reference to the three maple leaves. I do not intend to read the entire article but only the pertinent portion. He says:
This new flag design, with the maple leaves, throws the whole set-up out of kilter.
He is referring to the red ensign and "O Canada". He then goes on to say:
The design looks to me as something good for some group or organization, but not as a national symbol. However, to keep everything in focus, I have a suggestion for Mr. Pearson. If he is determined, and I respect his determination, to have the three maple leaves on a white background, with the two blue bars on the ends, then I suggest that he scrap "O Canada" in favour of "The Maple Leaf Forever" as the national anthem. At least this would be consistent. And one other thing. Since the proposed new flag has a large white field, it will be difficult to keep clean, once it hits the flag pole and starts to "brave the battle and the breeze". So, if the maple leaf design becomes the national flag, I suggested that Mr. Pearson make arrangements to have a package of "Breeze" given with every flag purchased. And let this be our rallying cry:
The maple leaf our emblem dear Upon our flag we sees.
With all our might We'll keep it white By using new blue Breeze.
I have made reference to that article, Mr. Speaker, to indicate some of the feeling toward the suggestion that this design is distinctively Canadian. Many of us have witnessed small flags on car radio aerials which are copies of the red ensign and the maple leaf design, and we have seen what a few weeks have done to them.
In reference to item 1 of the subamendment, Mr. Speaker, which deals with the Canadian red ensign, I received a very interesting letter from a retired army colonel. In this letter he refers to a visit to a tobacco shop operated by a Mr. John Dallas of New Glasgow. I might say that John Dallas is a well know merchant of Grecian origin who has lived in this town for many years. The letter in part states:
I was in his shop on Wednesday morning for my paper. He had a paper in his hand at the time. I

hardly got into the shop when he demanded to know, pointing to the red headlines on the flag issue, what do you think of that? Then he went on to say, there were two cuts on the front page, pointing to the Prime Minister's flag, "that is not my flag, this one is," meaning the red ensign, "it is the one I want, I will never put that so and so thing up," again pointing to the maple leaf design.
Mr. Speaker, that represents the feeling of only one citizen in this area who came to Canada many years ago and who operates a small shop in this community. That gentleman has been treated well by the town, country, province and indeed Canada. He expressed his feeling about this proposed design, and the red ensign. I fully endorse his views.
Shortly after receiving that letter I read an edition of the New Glasgow Evening News dated July 22, 1964 which contained an article in reference to this same Mr. John Dallas. That article reads as follows:
The philosophy of "don't throw away-save everything," has paid off for 81-year-old tobacco shop owner John Dallas.
Apparently this gentleman saved old cigarette packages which displayed various flags in existence as far back as 1914-15. The article then continues as follows:
Dead in the centre of the display is the flag of Canada, as yet-the red ensign.
As Mr. Dallas said, "That is the flag I want. I will never put that so and so thing up. The red ensign is my flag." And I, too, join with him and say the red ensign is my flag.
Many speeches have been made about letters received by members. I must state that I have received letters from members of Legion branches, branches of the I.O.D.E., the Silver Cross women and, indeed, from some younger people of my constituency, who endorse the red ensign.
As I pointed out, I hope that this problem will be solved soon. I hope the Prime Minister will withdraw the resolution so that the people of Canada may follow the procedure laid down by the subamendment and make their wishes known. As I told some of my colleagues, last night I was awakened at 1.30 by a telephone call from one of my constituents who was most irate about this matter. I assured him we were going into the matter fully. He was very disturbed. I hung up the phone, and at a quarter to two I received another call from him so I hope in heaven's name the Prime Minister does withdraw this resolution so that we can all have a little peace and quiet in this country.
