Canadian Flag
I slept on this matter, and this speech is the result.
In so far as the matter of the referendum is concerned, it can be pointed out-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What time did your caller call back that same night?

About 1.45. He still could not get to sleep. He was calling from Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, and he was very put out, as the Minister of Justice can well understand, not with Charlottetown but with the matter of the flag.
In so far as the matter of the referendum is concerned, perhaps I can just quote briefly from a newspaper article. The referendum, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) last night and the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) this afternoon, encompasses four different points. They are these: 1. Are you in favour of the red ensign? 2. Are you in favour of the red ensign with changes thereon to show the main heritage of the founding races? 3. Are you in favour of the three maple leaf design? 4. Are you in favour of the one maple leaf design? I think this subamendment should carry.
In so far as the referendum is concerned, as I have said perhaps I could quote briefly from the Globe and Mail for August 13, 1964.
Oh, oh.

I hear a little noise down in the corner there. The monkeys are at it again. I wish somebody would put them back in their cages and give them some peanuts to keep them quiet.
This article is by Bruce West, and reads in part as follows:
I am sure that many of us who now oppose the scrapping of our present proud flag would be willing to shut up and bow to the will of the majority if a referendum indicated that a new flag were desired by this country.
It might be painful, but not nearly so painful as the prospect of having this flag foisted upon us by a government which really gives its members no other choice but that of voting for the adoption of a new standard.
As I've often said here before-
Dispense.

This is very enjoyable; just listen.
-it seems to me that there is hardly any other question which deserves a free vote of the people more than that of what kind of flag they must live under.
The pertinent part follows:
Surely the democracy of which we have always been so proud hasn't fallen so low that such a

Canadian Flag
choice can't be made in a free and honourable manner. Once the referendum has been set up it would then be expected of all politicians that they would refrain from making any mention of the flag issue until after the people had expressed their will.
Any politician who attempted to inject the question into any of his harangues would then be clearly labelled for what he was-a tinhorn opportunist who was attempting to make capital out of a matter which should be considered above politics.
In this way we could probably preserve far more unity than under the present conditions, in which the flag issue can and does become a political football.
Then, there is this final paragraph:
Let the country speak on this matter. The answer will come from the soul, where it should come from when dealing with the question surrounded by such a great deal of honest sentiment. Once the country has spoken in this healthy manner, dissension on this subject will cease, no matter which way the vote may go.
As was pointed out in the issue of Labor of July 4, 1964, in a letter to the editor:
Prime Minister Lester Pearson has stirred up a hornets nest by wanting to destroy our lovely red ensign and put one of his own in its place, and what a tame thing his flag is. We already have maple leaves on the ensign. Our whole setup- Britain and the commonwealth-came from God's promise to Abraham in Genesis 33-11: "A nation and a company of nations shall be of thee."
Finally, as I have already stated, I am in favour of the red ensign and the subamendment which gives the people of Canada the opportunity to speak on this matter. The parliament of Canada cannot decide this issue since a free vote has not been accorded to all parliamentarians. I do not believe the present resolution before us will create the necessary unity in Canada. I have enjoyed the company of many of our friends from Quebec on many occasions. I have gone to army camps with them. I have been associated with many of them here in our House of Commons and I have enjoyed the House of Commons with them. I have enjoyed social occasions with them when we sang that old French Canadian song-not Alouette, that came later-The Regiment. I enjoyed that very much. I think there must be ways of further unifying this country other than the presentation of this resolution by the Prime Minister. Let him take cognizance of this. Let the government take cognizance of it. Let us go ahead so that in 1967 when we celebrate our 100th birthday we can show the necessary unity and we can fly a flag of which all Canadians can be justly proud.
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising is to-
Shorten the debate.

Perhaps, if that is possible, but especially to say something new in a debate which has been repetitious for some time now. It is also because I have young children and cannot afford to come here and listen for days on end to the speeches which the Conservatives seem likely to continue for the next several days.
Shame.

They are aware of the fact that the duty of the head of the family who has been elected a member of parliament is to sit in the house during several months and also be with his family when he can take a few days off. It could happen that I might not be in the house when votes are taken on minor questions, but I want my constituents and all the members of the house to know that I am in favour of a distinctive national flag and that I support the motion proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). In addition, if it was necessary to select a flag with a single maple leaf, green instead of red, with darker blue stripes, horizontal rather than vertical, I wish to say that I would still favour any such flag, as long as we finally select a distinctive national flag and bring this debate to a conclusion.
I understand some Conservative members are pleased to see more visitors in the public galleries during the summer than at any other time of the parliamentary year, but I feel rather ashamed that after 97 years of confederation and three years away from the centennial, we are still without a distinctive national flag. It seems to me that we should put an end to our discussions as soon as possible in order to be able to proudly hoist a fully Canadian flag.
As others pointed out earlier, we have nothing against the red ensign, or the French flag or still against the union jack, but we feel it is time, as I said in my speech of June 1, which is reported on page 3808 of Hansard, Canadians were proud enough of themselves, of their past, but also of their present achievements, to adopt their very own emblem.
Far be it from me to accuse those who take part in this debate with being dishonest and simply wanting to force their views on us. The matter is too serious and national unity is too important for me to accuse some members, regardless of their parties, with being dishonest or attempting to divide the country, because I am convinced that both sides are in favour of unity within the country. However, they do not all use the same

698S
means. Some resort to stronger action and others to gentler methods. I feel the motion put forward by the government is better suited to promote Canadian unity than the amendment proposed by the Conservative party.
Now, to come back to the subamendment, I think it is of no importance whatsoever whether the referendum includes one, four, ten or a hundred questions. A referendum is essentially an ultimate method of reaching a decision, one which can only be appropriate when there are no other means of settling a problem, especially when the decision put to the house would run counter to a commitment already made during an election campaign in respect of a well-defined policy.
We know that, in 1942, for instance, a referendum took place to release the government from one of its formal promises. Let us say it was a neat way to impose conscription on a group which wanted no part of it. That referendum was justified because the promise had been made, fallaciously or not, and the government wanted to be released from it.
If we were to pursue the argument of the Conservative party to absurdity, it would mean that no decision could be taken by parliament without a plebiscite being held.
Today, I heard the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) say that the government should be more respectful of democratic opinion. That is exactly why we were elected and it is because we live in a democratic country that we must take in the house a stand which meets the wishes of our constituents. Whether we spend a month, five months or a year discussing this matter, we will still be under the obligation to vote in the house, according to our conscience, it is true, but also according to the wishes of the majority of our constituents.
If the amendment proposed by the Conservatives had to do with the flag's shade of red or blue or the number of leaves, we could say that we have here an amendment on which to make a decision. But what is before us is a request to hold a referendum and the subamendment sets out in detail reasons for it which we could discuss forever. If we want democracy to prevail here in the House of Commons, the matter should be put to a vote. Let hon. members give their opinion in the house, let the electors know what it is, there is no objection to that, but let it be done after the vote, in the fall or later.
Canadian Flag
I am convinced that the house would give unanimous consent to let hon. members who have not had the opportunity to speak before adjournment to do so when the session resumes its normal course in the fall, provided that the vote is taken beforehand.
I say this because we know it is a most controversial matter and as there are 19 million people in the country, we will never reach a true solution. The only solution is to vote on the issue here in the house, because it will have to come to that sooner or later, even if the debate goes on for one or two years. In my opinion, that is what we should do, because after listening to all the arguments, I did not learn anything new about the referendum these past few days. Hon. members are only repeating the same arguments in a different way or quoting different newspaper editorials or taking ever so much time to explain why a certain stand will be taken. Now, filibustering is not serving the cause of the Conservatives or that of any other party. Every parliament is generally against resorting to a filibuster, even if it is a democratic or parliamentary procedure. It is a procedure which reminds me of the drowning person who will grab at anything, a dead leaf, a piece of wood, although knowing it is to no avail. But if the one who comes to his rescue realizes that the drowning person is trying to pull him under, he only has to hit him just hard enough to calm him down and bring him safely ashore.
I think hon. members have taken their stand and they now should vote accordingly.
I am therefore pleading with the Conservatives to stop their filibuster-or whatever they call this-stop prolonging this debate which, in any case, will end up by a vote being taken in a very democratic way.
We might in the same manner, have opposed the 11 per cent sales tax. We made representations and, finally, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) agreed to a compromise. He maintained the tax, but it started at 4 per cent and gradually escalated to 11 per cent. I realize that such a measure was unpopular; I know that other members could have extended the debate indefinitely until the minister should decide to withdraw it. But since the minister refused to withdraw the measure, the Conservatives decided after all to end the debate and to allow the question to be put, and this 11 per cent tax was passed.
I am sure that if the government were asked to use a little darker blue and to have smaller leaves, they would be prepared to

Canadian Flag
agree, because those are minor details, but to ask that a motion which has already been submitted to the house be completely changed, I think this is absolutely impossible, especially since the adoption of a flag was a promise made during the last electoral campaign by the party in office. Even we, of the Social Credit, had submitted a project which is different although it was a reasonable and clearly distinctive flag design.
We also know that the party in power finally accepted, after several about-turns, to bring nuclear arms into the country. Some members objected strenuously, but finally, the measure was passed and now certain formations of the Canadian army are equipped with nuclear armaments. Some were against it, and are still against it and always will be. But the measure was passed although for a time, the opposition played its role which was to prevent the government from getting nuclear arms, until it had exhausted all the reasonable and legitimate procedures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but it seems to me that after observing the rules of the house when he was talking about a plebiscite, he wandered away a great deal from the subject in the last few minutes.

Mr. Speaker, I was not dealing directly with the plebiscite, but with the consequences of the normal development of events which take place in this house, in a democratic way, because of the attitude of the members who were elected by the people.
I do not want to go farther, Mr. Speaker. I would like to quote several letters from voters who took the trouble to write to me-organizations like the St. Jean Baptiste society, the Jaycee's of Quebec city, the students of Laval University-and ask me to fight tooth and nail in favour of the flag proposed by the government.
I do not want to delay any longer the debates of the house, but I say that several persons and organizations wrote and asked me to support the measure introduced by the government, which is consonant with my personal opinion, so that it is twice as easy.
In conclusion, I will relate a fact-I hope that you will allow me to do so, Mr. Speaker -which happened last year during the international scout jamboree held in Greece; if my memory is good, it was near Athens, but I am not sure. The Canadian scouts were represented by various units coming from different parts of the country. There was namely a unit from the province of Quebec, and the

government of that province had given its scouts the fleur-de-lis flag in order to show that the were from the province of Quebec.
All Canadian scouts were quartered together. Suddenly, an English scout decided to organize a display of flags; a British scout decided to have a display of all the flags. He went around all the units asking them to come for a parade with their own distinctive national flag. When he came to the Canadian unit, he said to the leader of the Quebec company: Come in with your flag: Canada must parade with its flag. The scout replied: But this is not Canada's flag, it is the flag of the province of Quebec. The other asked: Where is the Canadian flag? The scout answered: It is the other over there. The scout leader retorted: But it is not that one; this one is everybody's. We want a distinctive flag.
He then asked the Quebec company to take part in the display with the Quebec flag.
That means that even the British people, who have undoubtedly great respect for the Queen and the traditions, realize, when they see the flag which is presently considered as Canada's flag, that it is not a distinctive flag, and they insist on Canadians having a flag which would distinguish them from the British group.
Mr. Speaker, I will not dwell any longer on that matter. I merely wanted to change the atmosphere a little to show that, in spite of all, we want to co-operate with the government, not because we like the flag as such, but because it is a distinctive flag.
To conclude, I submit that the official opposition should not force the government to avail itself of standing order 33 which is the closure rule, nor of standing order 52, which is the rule concerning the previous question.
With all the consideration I have for the Conservative members who oppose the flag and with all the consideration I have for those who have taken part in the debate on the students loans legislation in a rather lengthy fashion, I think that we must finally come to a decision and that the government would not be blamed, in these circumstances, if they introduce a motion to apply the rule of closure. I am sure that if any member of the house could do it, this motion would be introduced, perhaps right now.
I therefore, suggest to the government that, if the opposition continues its filibuster, its extension of the debate, it should take its responsibilities and move to apply either section 51 of standing orders which deals with

the previous question, or section 33 which deals with closure of debates.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, if he allows me to do so.
I should like to know whether the hon. member can answer this question: Does the fact that a member of the house, even though he is a Conservative, uses a privilege reserved to any member of the House of Commons, that is the privilege to speak, as the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency has just done, mean that he is filibustering? As a matter of fact, I have not yet spoken and I intend to do so before the end of the debates.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to answer the hon. member's question. Nobody is deprived of the right to speak, but this is simply a normal resolution brought forward in the usual fashion and which is discussed usually in a reasonable number of days and finally put to the vote.
Then, under those circumstances, it happens that a number of members, from each party, are designated to speak-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that the subject matter of the discussion between the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency is somewhat different from the subject now before the house.

Would the hon. member
allow me to ask him a question about the referendum?
Yes, provided the house allows me to answer it.

Would the hon. member answer the following question?
On March 17, 1962, when the hon. member still belonged to the Social Credit party, his former leader, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) stated that if his party assumed office, he would hold a referendum on the flag issue within six months following his coming to office.
Was the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency in favour of that commitment? If not, why did he not denounce it at that time?
To my knowledge, the leader of the Social Credit party at the time had not made such a statement.

I think at the outset I should read, or place before the house, exactly what it is I propose to talk
Canadian Flag
about tonight. My speech will of course be circumscribed by Your Honour's ruling of yesterday, but I should like to put the amendment on record again. It reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" in line one be deleted and the following substituted:
"As the proposal to change Canada's national flag will affect the unity and destiny of Canada now and for years to come, the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to conduct a plebiscite prior to any further action being taken by the House of Commons, in order that all Canadians may be given their rightful opportunity to declare their choice concerning a national flag."
This was later the subject of a further amendment by my hon. friend from Regina City (Mr. More) who moved:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the words:
"and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
This is the ambit of the discussion at the present time.
I wish to say right now, Mr. Speaker, where I stand on this question. First, I am in favour of the subamendment providing for a plebiscite, with the four questions set out to allow people to express exactly what they want to vote for. I am also in favour of the continuance of the Canadian red ensign as Canada's national flag. I want to tell you right now, Mr. Speaker, exactly why I am in favour of our red ensign continuing as Canada's national flag. In the first place, it has been Canada's flag for many years. It is a flag that has been carried and honoured all over the world. It is a distinctive flag, because no other nation in the world has a flag that looks like the red ensign. It has been said that New Zealand's flag, Australia's flag and the flags of several other countries are the same; but they are not-they have blue ensigns. There is not another national flag in the world that looks like the Canadian red ensign.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I represent a constituency that is made up of 70 per cent central Europeans. We have there about 40 different national origins. Thirty thousand of the people whom I represent are of Ukrainian, Polish, Czechoslovakian, Austrian and Rumanian origin, including also the other

Canadian Flag
central European countries. I represent about 6,100 people of Anglo-Saxon origin, about 1,300 people of French origin, nearly 3,000 people of German origin, and the rest are made up of other national origins of 40 different countries.
In the last election campaign I held about 45 election meetings. At every meeting where the flag became an issue or was talked about at all I was asked where I stood on the flag question. I said, "Naturally, being a veteran, belonging to the Royal Canadian Legion, and being a Canadian, I stand for the Canadian red ensign as Canada's flag". Whenever the flag was mentioned and I made that statement I received the applause of everybody at the meeting, of whatever national origin they happened to be. I was told by Americans that this was the only stand to take. Thousands of Ukrainian people have told me they came to this country from their homeland because they did not have freedom there. They came to this country and found freedom under the union jack. They have told me that any flag which did not bear the union jack on it somewhere was no good for them.
I have, as a matter of fact, some 1,300 native Canadian Indians in my constituency. These people look on the union jack-the red ensign now-as the Queen, the person with whom their treaties were made, the great white mother. They want to see a flag with a union jack on it; it has to be the Canadian red ensign or some modification thereof. They prefer it as it is but, like the rest of us who are reasonable people, will certainly make a concession to the rest of the people if others want a maple leaf or a fleur-de-lis or something else on the flag. But the first choice is the Canadian red ensign, as is.
Carried.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to mention Quebec at all, but I just want to say right now that I thank the good God that the whole of Quebec is not represented by people like these who are yapping all the time. Whenever a person gets up to speak in English, these people are yapping. They talk about our dividing the country, but when we have something to say and get up to say it, they interfere all the time. It is they who are dividing this country, and not us.
Order.
Yes; you can yell "Order" till you are black in the face.

It does not matter-
