speechtext: Order. I think when the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Fane) began his remarks he was completely within the ambit of the motion before us. I would suggest that he continue in that vein.

Mr. Speaker, I never intended to get off the track at all. As you know, when I am told what the limitations are, I usually stick to them; but when remarks are passed such as those that have been passed, I naturally have to reply. There is another thing about the Canadian red ensign. I have travelled a great deal around the country. I was recently in the United States. I travelled to-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Texas.
No, I didn't go to Texas. I didn't go to Kootenay East either. Perhaps some time the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) will be big enough to stand on his feet and make his own speech.
Hear, hear.
He sits there and "byrnes".

I was a member of a committee of this house that went to Colorado Springs, the headquarters of the air force section of NORAD. It was a very great pleasure to see the Canadian red ensign flying beside old glory on a flagstaff of equal size. It was certainly very wonderful to see our flag there.

The same situation prevailed in Norfolk, Virginia, and in Bermuda. I was recently at a Rotary convention in the city of Toronto. There were around 16,000 people there; they were mostly from the United States. When they saw from the badge I was wearing that I was a Canadian they said, "You are a Canadian. What do you think about this flag issue?"
Fortunately I did not have to go into too much detail, but I told them that there was no issue, that it should not be an issue because it was entirely phony. I said the majority of the people of Canada wanted to continue with the red ensign, but this government had decided that the flag should be changed. These people said to me: "Why in the name of heaven would anybody want to change that beautiful flag which you now have?" That is the way the Americans feel about the Canadian red ensign. Naturally I did not talk to all 16,000 who were there, but I did personally talk to about 200 people from the United States, which I think is a pretty good cross section. Other people were there from all parts of the world and I talked to many of them, and they felt the same way about the matter.
As I said a minute ago, the flag issue seems to be very unnecessary at this time because it was not an election issue. Certainly it appeared in the platform of the Liberal party that within two years of election a Liberal government would submit to parliament a design for a flag which could not be mistaken for the emblem of any other country. If they had done that there might be something to say for it, but they did not. The flag proposed by the government, with the exception of the maple leaves, is almost exactly the same as the flag of the republic of Guatemala. I might also point out, quoting my hon. friend from Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood), that the proposed flag is not too much different from the merchant marine flag of the Soviet union. It has the same colours; it has red in the middle and a white background. Therefore, how can anyone think that the flag presented by the Prime Minister is distinctive, that there is no other flag like it? That proposition is fallacious. Are we to give up the flag which has had its beginnings as the flag of the British merchant navy for a flag not too different in looks from the Soviet merchant navy flag? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what are we coming to? What is the outlook of a Prime Minister who would bring into this house a flag like that, and try to ram it down the throats of par-
Canadian Flag
liament and impose it on the people of Canada? That is exactly what is happening here, Mr. Speaker.
That is why this party is so opposed to this flag. It was not a definite election promise. Only a few people referred to it. In my constituency it was not a general issue in the last election, and the people were not told what kind of flag they would be asked to accept. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that 90 per cent of the people in my constituency will not accept this proposed flag. If we held a plebiscite I would venture to say that 90 per cent of my people would vote entirely for the red ensign.
During my visits back home I meet a great many people, and since the question of the flag has become an issue only three people have said to me that we should accept the flag proposed by the Prime Minister. One of these people was a man who originated in Quebec, one was a man who originated in Poland and the other was a man from Scotland. They told me they would accept this proposed flag, and they are the only three constituents out of 45,000 who have openly supported this flag. The rest of the people have said to me: "Go ahead and get the Canadian red ensign continued as our flag. If you cannot do anything else about it, then if possible get a plebiscite and let us vote, because so far we have not had a chance to say whether we want a different flag from the one we now have. The way we feel is that no flag without the union jack on it is any good for us".
These people are also wondering, as I am, what force impelled the Prime Minister to bring this flag issue to the fore at this time when it was unnecessary to do so. The Prime Minister has lots of other election promises which remain unfulfilled and are more important to the economy of the country than changing our national flag. Was somebody blackmailing him? Why did he pass it on to parliament? That is what the people want to know. They say: "Why fight an election on the flag issue? We will be forced to vote for the candidate who supports the flag we want, whether we like him or not". That is another reason the flag should not be made an election issue. These people are also wondering why the Prime Minister did not first unveil his flag in the House of Commons, in parliament. That is why we are here. If we are to pass judgment on this flag and to decide under which flag we should live, we should have been the first to hear about it and to see it. We were told this

Canadian Flag
afternoon about all the devious ways in which it was unveiled before being presented to the house.
I was at the annual convention of the Royal Canadian Legion in Winnipeg and I heard the Prime Minister put forth his ideas about what should be our national flag. He did not get very much support. It was unfortunate, but the reason he did not get a good hearing was that the initial opening ceremony at conventions of the Royal Canadian Legion is a sacred one. It is a ceremony of dedication to those Canadians who did not come back from the wars. These people feel that the Prime Minister has desecrated their sacred service.
Mr. Speaker, I have told you why I support the red ensign and why I do not support the flag proposed by this government. I have indicated that I would settle for a modification of the red ensign if the adoption of such a modification would unite Canada. I do not believe a flag containing three maple leaves or, for that matter, containing one maple leaf would be adequate and assist in uniting this country.
If we desire to have a flag containing national symbols, why do we not include a symbol representative of those citizens who lived in this country before the white people came? Surely we should have something representative of those Canadians we see fit to call North American Indians.
There have been suggestions made in respect of members serving in the armed forces in Canada under the symbol of a maple leaf. Of the 34 years I was in the service I wore the maple leaf on my uniform for only two years. For the remaining period of time my badge depicted either a beaver or a horse. I think too much consideration has been given to the use of the maple leaf by the armed services.
I suggest the government should give consideration to the amendment proposed by the opposition and hold a plebiscite on this national flag issue. I think by following that course the government will obtain the opinion of the people of Canada and avoid any future argument. Certainly some segments of the population will be in favour of the new flag while others will be in favour of the retention of the Canadian red ensign as it now appears or as modified. I think the only way out of this impasse is a plebiscite which would allow the people of Canada to come to a decision in respect of a Canadian national flag. The people of Canada have not had an opportunity of voting on this flag issue; whether we should

have a national flag, or whether we should change our present flag. I do not suggest that we hold an election-and I do not make that statement because I am afraid to face my electors.
I am quite sure the other members of my party are not afraid of the results of an election, but I am sure that if an election is held the flag issue will be obscured and the end result will not be clear. For that reason I say we must have a plebiscite containing those questions suggested by the subamendment.
Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested by some members on the government side that the member for Regina City (Mr. More) should not have moved the subamendment to the amendment moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. I am sure that had the government offered a plebiscite it would contain the question: Do you prefer the flag proposed by this government or would you rather have one covered with pink polliwogs on a rainbow rampant? There would have been no choice offered. The population would be in the same position the backbenchers on the government side find themselves in at this time. The Prime Minister has said that he would consider an adverse vote on this flag issue as reason for an election and the defeat of his government. That is why his members support his proposal. While I do not shed any tears for them because they are all free, white and 21 and have made this decision with their eyes open, I would hate to be in their shoes at the time of the next election, having backed the proposal for a new flag which displaced the Canadian red ensign.
I have only referred to the Canadian Legion as being in support of the retention of the Canadian red ensign as the national flag, but there are innumerable associations also in favour of that retention. I have also referred to the many letters I have received from my constituents who are in favour of the retention of the red ensign. I have not received one letter from one constituent expressing support for the government proposed national flag.
I have received letters from other parts of Canada. In fact, I have a pile one and a half feet high on my file tables. I am very pleased to have received those letters and have attempted to reply to them all, but this is an onerous task. Some of those letters have been in favour of the new proposed flag.
I wish the Prime Minister was now in his seat because I should like to suggest to him that he should recall the final four lines of

the poem "In Flanders Fields" written by the late Colonel John McCrae. I do not think it is necessary for me to quote it but I will do so for the benefit of those who are not familiar with the words.
To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high.
If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
I would ask the Prime Minister how in the name of heaven on November 11, Remembrance day, he is going to be able to say along with the rest of the veterans: "In the morning and at the going down of the sun we will remember them".
Thank you.

Carried.
Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton North and
Victoria): Mr. Speaker, I hear some hon. members across the way crying "carried". I hear some hon. members on my left saying "let us vote". I do not believe that these members who say these things deep down in their hearts, believe that those who feel they have a duty to express their thoughts on this subject should not do so.
In rising to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I realize it is most difficult to make an original contribution on a subject that has already absorbed the attention of the house and has resulted in some of the finest contributions to debate since I became a member of this house in 1957. I should like to refer specifically to the speech made today by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), and in the earlier debate to the speeches delivered by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). I rise, Mr. Speaker, because this is a subject which touches the hearts and minds of many Canadians and crosses party lines, or indeed should cross party lines. Last Sunday afternoon I attended an outdoor church service. As I was leaving the grounds where this service was held I saw a very good friend of mine. I say that he is a good friend, but on election day he does his best for the Liberal party in an effort to defeat me. I jokingly said to him, "I am leaving for Ottawa in a couple of hours, is there a message you would like me to take to Mr. Pearson?" He said, "Yes, there is. You tell that man to put his flag in mothballs and put it away." You can see, therefore, that a subject like this does cross party lines. This man, while a good friend, is not a supporter of mine, and I doubt if he ever will be because if one knows the traditions
Canadian Flag
in some areas he realizes that people do not change their political affiliations.
We have before us a subamendment which provides the means whereby Canadians can make a selection from what appears to be the more acceptable flag designs submitted. If I were to vote in such a plebiscite with four choices, I would choose the Canadian red ensign. However, I am democratic enough that I am willing to put my personal choice to the test. The question in my mind, and in the minds of many Canadians, is why the government is unwilling to put its personal choice to the test.
It is.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
But not in the form of a plebiscite. Let us not become confused about the meaning of importance and urgency. While I consider no subject of greater importance to the Canadian nation than the selection of a flag I, at the same time, associate no great urgency with its selection. The greatest danger facing this house at the moment is what the end result of thoughtless haste might be. The government would be well advised to remove this subject from debate in this chamber and provide a cooling off period, while carrying on with the more urgent matters facing this house and the country.
A few days ago I had the very great pleasure of taking part in the annual Gaelic mod at St. Ann's in my constituency at which time, as usual, the Scots met together to demonstrate to the world that they have kept faith with their historic past. Now, is this not the crux of this debate? Is not the objective of the official opposition to try to convince the government that the flag approved by the members of this house should be one which keeps faith with our historic past?
Canada is a nation composed of many cultures, many traditions, all of which have contributed to the strength, the diversity and the unity that make our country unique. In order to be vibrant, to be forward looking, to be progressive, a country must foster a national pride and love of country; must cherish its traditions and base its progress on what has proven of value in the past. So it is with Canada. The many races that are today an inherent part of Canada have enriched our culture and developed our economy. We have only to look around us here to see the proof of that statement.
I am reminded of the annual Dominion day celebrations here in Ottawa when the lawn in front of the parliament buildings echoes to
6S92

Canadian Flag
the songs and dances of many nationalities, originally brought from distant lands but which now form an integral part of the colourful mosaic that is the Canadian way of life. These are the traditional things which are prized by groups individually and by nations collectively. These are the inherent strains of our Canadians nation which we must strive to preserve and protect. These are the elements, Mr. Speaker, which make Canada distinctive, for without these distinctive elements Canada would soon lose something of its appeal, its very reason for being. Each and every one of us has a responsibility to preserve what has proven of value in the past, for we of this generation are the channel through which our traditions and cultures will be passed to the rising generation. Canadians of Scottish origin, particularly Cape Breton Scots, have diligently discharged their responsibilities in this regard.
As a Scot representing the constituency of Cape Breton North and Victoria, I would be remiss in what I consider my responsibilities if I did not participate in the debate on a subject of this importance, and speak out against any government, no matter of what political party, which by its actions would eliminate all traces of our historic past in proposing a flag design such as is embodied in the resolution before us. Think for a moment of our history. The earliest settlers of Cape Breton came from France and our island became the jewel in the French crown, the Gibraltar of the north. Indeed, at the height of its fame as a French colony, Cape Breton was known as Isle Royale, the royal island. Years later there was an influx of Scottish settlers, some 30,000 strong, and they utilized their traits of perseverance, integrity and love of country to build upon the foundations of the earlier French settlements. These two strains, the French peasant and the highland crofter, are still strong in Cape Breton. Together, they have made our island a place of unique interest to the many visitors who come to our shores. They have done this by preserving their traditions and promoting their culture as a part of their everyday life.
Then, think for a moment of the history of Canada. The pattern of development in Cape Breton can well be applied to the country as a whole. You will recall that it was the French who first established settlements along the shores of the St. Lawrence and who later made their way by canoe and foot into the unknown interior, opening up the great fur trade upon which the early economy of the country was based. We do well to remember 
their struggles, their trials and their tribulations in this field under almost impossible conditions.
But it awaited the contribution of the Scottish highlanders to transform the fur trade into an industrial development of fire, imagination and boldness which took traders and explorers all the way from our eastern shores to the gulf of Mexico and to the Pacific and Arctic oceans. The Scottish characteristics of daring and tenacity complemented the know how and perseverance of the French voyageur and the result was, in large measure, a great new country.
The early French and Scottish settlers showed their willingness and their adaptability to work together for the common good. Of all the contributions made towards the successful building of this nation, none have been greater than the efforts of these two races. And to their credit, down through the years they have striven to preserve their own cultures and their own traditions. Our annual Gaelic mods to which I referred earlier, are a good example of the success of the Scots in this regard.
In these days, when strife and conflict characterize many actions and reactions in Canada, let us not forget the enrichment to
our society by the many other groups who have come to these shores seeking a new home. Each group has made its contribution and the country is the greater for it; the loss of even one would leave Canada a poorer nation. In my constituency, where we once had only the French and Scots, we today find people representative of every ethnic group in this nation. These people have indicated an appreciation of the contribution made by the French and Scots to the development of our area and, at the same time, the French and Scots have derived great benefit and diversity through the infusion of these groups, that has added lustre to the development of our area and its culture and traditions. They have together, I feel, developed reverence for the Canadian red ensign and what it stands for.
Unfortunately, there is a tendency by some in this country today to discount and discredit the traditions, symbols and cultures which constitute the Canadian mosaic. We must not let ourselves be swayed by this lack of awareness of the things that have made Canada great and which will keep her great. We must not be lulled into allowing our interest to weaken or our fervour to abate in our devotion to the things we hold dear.

I am not, nor have I ever been, a flag waver. I must confess I did not discuss the flag question during the last election campaign or any other campaign, but then neither did my Liberal opponent, nor anyone else on either side, so far as I am aware. I do not feel the voters of my constituency or, indeed, of this nation, expressed their opinion on this flag question during the last campaign. I am in favour of keeping the Canadian red ensign as our national flag because it keeps faith with our historic past. At the .same time, and because this was not discussed during the last election campaign, I am unwilling to allow the government to make a decision for me or for my constituents on a new flag design, until I know their feelings on our present distinctive flag.
Some speakers have mentioned letters they received, and representations which were made to them. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I have received many communications but only one of them was in favour of the proposed new flag. If I were to go by the mail I have received I would of course vote for the Canadian red ensign, but through the process of a plebiscite the people of my constituency would have an opportunity to say what they favour, as would people elsewhere throughout the country; and if the majority were in favour of the proposed new flag then I would be the first to honour forever whatever new flag the majority favoured.
How can any one man, or small committee of individuals, select a flag for 19 million people without first endeavouring to ascertain from them whether they desire any alteration or change in our present flag? The plebiscite now requested by the official opposition and the choices suggested in the subamendment are in my mind the more democratic approach for selecting a flag, and I approve of this approach and will vote for it when that moment arises.
Why should there be any objection to this subamendment or, indeed, to the amendment in relation to a plebiscite? We are not a people who have been held in political or economic bondage within the British commonwealth and, as a result, had any sign or symbol which reminds us of colonial rule. We are a nation which developed through political evolution. We are a living example to the world that it is possible for a colonial possession to become an independent nation. Not for us was there a war to achieve independence; not for us was there violence or the threat of violence. Since we did cut our colonial ties in an orderly manner, there was
Canadian Flag
no oppressor, no feeling of casting off the bonds of an evil oppressor, no feeling that we must wipe away any sign or symbol from our national life which would remind us of a time when we were not free. Quite the contrary, I think it can be freely said that Canadians have a feeling of respect and of good will towards the homelands of their ancestors. I do not believe they wish to tear out of their flag, which has evolved with our growth to nationhood, all references to their past.
We are not a people who are ashamed of our beginnings. I do not think we are a people who want to put some kind of a blackout over our past, as if we did not know our ancestry or that we were ashamed of it. And I do not believe Canadians are the kind of people so haunted by feelings of inferiority that they must proclaim they belong to a free and independent state.
Let us have a plebiscite on this question. Let us get the views of the Canadian people in a free, democratic manner. Let the people of Canada decide whether they feel a new flag is in the interest of national unity; let them decide whether a new flag would give them a sense of pride in their country.
Personally, I believe Canadians now have a sense of pride in their country and have confidence in its future. If they do not, then I do not think all the flags in the world would give them a proper sense of pride and of confidence. Any sense of pride and confidence a flag could possibly give would then be a false and phoney pride and unworthy of our Canadian people. Mr. Speaker, there is but one sure, certain way to obtain the views of Canadians on this question: A plebiscite is the answer.
A flag which is going to fly over us and which will command our loyalty, devotion and sacrifice-yes, our lives, if need be-should be a flag that is born in the hearts of its citizens and reflects the best and truest in all of us, and that speaks for the people, because the people spoke for it. And then it would not be Pearson's personal preference, a political platform promise, or a pennant pushed through parliament by a prejudiced party.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to take the opportunity of assuring you, sir, that my remarks this evening on this subject will be on point, constructive, not provocative or repetitive and, I hope, persuasive. The first question I think we should consider on the subamendment is the basic one of whether a plebiscite

Canadian Flag
is justified. This is a question which has been asked a great many times in this house during the present debate. I have assured you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to be repetitive, and since I did discuss this matter at some length in the course of my remarks on the amendment on July 2 last, I do not intend to repeat what I said on that occasion. However, I think a brief summation might be in order.
I think it is clear to all students of government, and of parliamentary government in particular, that while in most circumstances members of parliament are sent here to decide public issues-I would say this is true in at least 99 per cent of all instances-* there are always exceptions in human institutions and there are certain times when a plebiscite or referendum is clearly justified. These are instances where members of parliament do not have at their disposal any special knowledge or information which their constituents lack. This, of course, is the case when moral or emotional issues are involved -issues such as capital punishment, for example, the use or non-use of alcohol, or a decision about a national flag as in the present instance. In none of these cases do members of this house have any greater knowledge of the subject concerned than do their constituents. Consequently, they cannot, in a sense, act as representatives at all, and such matters are fit ones for a plebiscite.
This afternoon, when the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Willoughby)- was speaking, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) asked him if he disagreed with the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) who, at one time, it was alleged had objected to a referendum being placed before the Canadian people. I am surprised that the Minister of Justice, who is such an eminent member of the Canadian bar, would not have shown more discernment in a matter such as this. The subject he referred to was, I take it, the referendum on conscription held during the second world war. It is clear that in a case such as that, members of parliament have a great deal more information at their disposal, both confidential and otherwise, than do their constituents and for this reason a referendum would be unsatisfactory. In fact I think it proved to be so.
It has been said during this debate that the discussion has gone on too long. The word "filibuster" has been used repeatedly.
Oh, no.

In the first place, the word "filibuster" is a word which Canadians have

borrowed from the United States. It is quite unsuitable to apply to our parliamentary government and it has a connotation, from things we read in the United States press and things which actually go on in the United States congress, which has no application to the affairs of this country in the sense in which it is used. In any event, a filibuster is justified in certain circumstances, whether in the United States or in Canada. It is most certainly justified when a minority government attempts to force down the throat of parliament what is apparently-and I will come to this in a moment-a proposal which commands the support of only a minority of Canadians. I can think of no instance when a filibuster would be more justified, if such were the case.
During this long debate-and it will probably continue for a while-the public discussion which has gone on both in this house and outside on this important subject has been I think very valuable. This is something which has in my opinion been overlooked by many who have taken part in the discussion. We have seen a great number of criticisms in public media of information and elsewhere saying: Get the flag issue decided; get it out of the way; sweep it under the rug; it is costing too much money; it is taking the place of things of more value, pension schemes and the like. I do not know what we are coming to in this country when we place a dollars and cents value on every subject which comes up. I am shocked at the extent of criticism of this kind. It proves we have no moral values any longer in this country; everything is calculated in dollars and cents and if you cannot place a dollar value on something it is not worth discussing. Well, in my opinion there are many things of great value to which a dollar label cannot be attached. The symbols of our country and of what we stand for and the principles we choose to follow are among such things. Some of the shallow criticism we find in the press from pseudo-intellectuals who edit our press-and I think of the Ottawa Citizen in this connection, among others-should be reconsidered.
In this regard there are three important and constructive things which have come out of our discussion. First, it has been shown that a large percentage of the people of Canada are very interested in the subject of a Canadian flag regardless of their views as to what its design should be, or should not be. The people are interested in whatever is to symbolize our country, and in what we

stand for. This is good. It is a matter of great importance and value. Everyone will agree, I think, that any flag design must command at least a majority of public support. The discussion has clearly shown, I think, as a result of the work of the press, Gallup polls, and the like, that apparently no present flag which is much in the public eye has more than, at the best, the support of 40 per cent of the people of this country. I refer to an article which appeared recently on the front page of Le Droit, and a column by Mr. Patrick Nicholson. The figures he gave, and I have not heard them refuted, showed that of all the provinces of Canada the province of Quebec offered most support for any design, but even this amounted to not more than 40 per cent, in all Canada. The red ensign had a majority of support-a small one, perhaps-in the other nine provinces, and it came second in Canada with a substantial 30-odd per cent. Apparently neither of these flags have a majority of public support behind them.
The discussion has led to a better understanding of the points of view of members of this house as well as of the points of view of others throughout the country. I know it has helped me a great deal. I do not agree with all that other speakers have said during this debate, but at least I have a better understanding of their views now than I did before the debate started. So I think these are three constructive things which have resulted from this debate.
There is one most unfortunate thing which has resulted from this debate and it is something most of us deplore. As a result of these discussions, both in this house and in the country, a great deal of bitterness has been engendered. The debate has been divisive in many ways and that is a most unfortunate thing. But, after all, it is the government which is responsible for having initiated this debate at this time and it is the government which must take full responsibility for the unfortunate aspect I have mentioned.
Since it appears that only a minority of the people of Canada support any flag design, we in this house should all know the real facts of the matter before parliament makes a decision and the only way in which this can be done is by means of a plebiscite. A referendum is too binding on any government; the holding of a plebiscite is the way to go about it. Then we would have the real facts instead of the educated guesses of public opinion pollsters. If we had a plebiscite, parliament could properly decide its course of
Canadian Flag
action. After such a plebiscite, the Prime Minister himself might be a little less unrelenting and adamant with regard to the position he has taken.
I realize there are difficulties attached to drawing up the proper question to be placed before the electorate in a matter of this kind. But the four questions that appear in the subamendment are perhaps the only possible or logical ones that could be presented to the public in this regard.
The first question in the subamendment concerns the red ensign. This is of course one of the very logical flags to place as a choice before the electorate. This is the flag we have had for quite a number of years. We have had it officially as the flag of Canada since 1946, which is something a large number of the public do not seem to realize at all. Is it a distinctive flag? I think it is, in a great many ways, and a great many other people do also. This flag is very highly regarded and very much wanted in many parts of Canada. I agree that certain regions wish it more than others, and some regions do not wish it at all, apparently. I conducted a little plebiscite of my own in my region, and 75 per cent to 80 per cent of the people, at a minimum, would like to see the red ensign retained. But I also found in my own area that people are not that rigid. They would prefer the red ensign to be retained, but I found that people in our part of the country are flexible and reasonable and I think would meet the viewpoint of other people in this country if that should prove necessary.
Also, Mr. Speaker, people in other parts of the country have very deep feelings-this also applies to my own area-on the subject of the red ensign. It is something under which they have been raised; it is something that symbolizes to them our institutions of parliamentary government, freedom of speech, the courts. You cannot just disregard people's views in this matter, because they are very sincerely held views. Then, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) this afternoon, who came to Canada at a very young age and is of Ukrainian origin and this applies to other members of so-called ethnic groups, which is a term I do not really care for very much, Mr. Speaker -these people are very fond of the red ensign because they made Canada the country of their own choice; they came here because, as was so eloquently pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for On-

Canadian Flag
tario, of the institutions for which the red ensign stands. For this reason, because the red ensign is so strongly viewed as a symbol of Canada in the hearts of so many people -well over 30 per cent-this is clearly one choice that should appear on a plebiscite.
The second question concerns a modified form of the red ensign. This has come about as a result of public discussion of this matter, which I mentioned a few moments ago. This has been a very valuable result of the considerable discussion on this matter. I know this modified version of the red ensign is a matter of personal preference. I would prefer to see something of this nature myself. This would be my first choice, although if a vote did come in this house I feel obliged to support the red ensign because that is the wish of my constituents; and to be logical in my discussion that must be my stand. But as a purely personal choice I would like to see some modified version of the red ensign to bring together as other hon. members have mentioned the symbols of the two principal cultural groups in this country. I believe these things are necessary in order for a flag to be meaningful. A flag that is invented out of thin air so to speak, or as a result of some pedantic thinking, some sort of deep delving into abstruse subjects in producing designs is sometimes not the best method. It may have real meaning in the heraldic sense, but from a practical, common sense point of view it may have very little meaning.
The next question on the subamendment is of course concerned with the maple leaves flag which has been suggested by the Prime Minister and his party. I think most of us are aware that probably the very, very large majority of people in the province of Quebec prefer this flag. Most of us understand, as a result of public discussion of this matter over some period of time, why the people of Quebec prefer to see a flag design which does not incorporate the union jack. I do not agree with them but I can understand their point of view. I sympathize with them without agreeing, because I can understand their point of view. They feel the union jack is a symbol of something rather unpleasant in the past. I also know that the suggestion that there be the fleur-de-lis on a modified red ensign is something that is objected to and I can understand why it is objected to. It is because to some people it represents, to put it in the vernacular, the letting down by the Bourbon kings in 1759. I can understand why neither of these symbols would be particularly agreeable to the people of Quebec,

and I think most of us can understand this as a result of public discussion both here and elsewhere. There is, of course, certain support in other parts of Canada for the flag presented by the Prime Minister. It has not as much support as has the red ensign, but it has substantial support. I think we must all recognize that fact. For this reason, most certainly the flag presented by the Prime Minister and his party should be on any plebiscite to be held.
The fourth item is the question of a single maple leaf flag, which is really a modified version of the Prime Minister's suggestion. That design has appeared before this house, in the press and elsewhere as a result of lengthy public discussion. Since there is apparently some considerable following for this design-how much, we do not know, but I believe most of us have received representations and letters to this effect-this likewise is a design that should appear on the plebiscite.
When the real results of public opinion are known as a result of a plebiscite-and this is the only way in which it can be known- we will be in a much better position to decide upon a flag design. There is no other way of determining public opinion in this regard, apart from educated guessing by pollsters, which does not mean very much; very many people tell pollsters they have no opinion because they feel they are not expressing the opinion that is expected of them. A good example of this occurred recently in connection with the California primaries in the United States election. There were supposed to be so many undecided people, but they clearly were not at all undecided; they supported Senator Goldwater. They thought this was perhaps not the popular thing to say at the time, but that is what they were going to do.
I believe that on an emotional issue such as the flag many people will not say what they want to do; they want to keep their opinions to themselves; they do not want to get into quarrels with their neighbours and so many other people. For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I believe the results of a plebiscite might be very surprising. Anything else would be merely guessing, and the only way to ascertain the wishes of the people is by holding a plebiscite. If a plebiscite is held, we will have some real results in this house upon which to base our opinions and our final decision. Then I think perhaps even the

Prime Minister might revise his opinions on what he should do.
If the plebiscite showed that a large majority, or even a substantial majority of the people of Canada supported any design, no matter what it was, I believe any member of this house would be very glad to support that flag design and accept it as the Canadian flag. This would then be an end of the matter. Eut if no majority should appear, not even a simple majority, for any one flag as a result of such a plebiscite, another course of action would have to be taken.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

I certainly respect the
fairness of the hon. member's presentation. Does the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) consider that the method used in 1921 by Mr. Meighen to adopt arms, and the method used by Mr. King in 1945 to adopt a flag, namely order in council, was inappropriate or undemocratic; and would that method be appropriate today?

The method used on occasions in the past may well have been appropriate for those conditions, but at the present time I do not feel those conditions would be at all appropriate. Here there is public controversy over the matter whereas on the other occasions there was not. One must adjust to the times.
No, there is not.

The hon. member for Mercier iMr. Boulanger) may feel there is no public controversy, but he must be living in a rather rarefied ivory tower, to say the least. If it was found from such a plebiscite that there was not even a simple majority for any flag-and I really cannot understand why government members seem so sure about this, yet are alarmed at the thought of a plebiscite-then I would suggest that a parliamentary committee, consisting, say, of ten members drawn from all parties on an appropriate basis, be set up to try and decide on a flag design. Although I realize there are some who would not agree, I feel that a time limit should be set of three to four months. Then that parliamentary committee, knowing the real feelings of the people as a result of the plebiscite, could get together with such a time limit and work out some compromise design which might be mutually unsatisfactory to every-
Canadian Flag
one, as it is said, but might be reasonably satisfactory to most people in Canada.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
The hon. member has referred to the possibility of there not being a majority.

No, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid I do not agree with my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson). I do not normally disagree with him but on this occasion I do. I feel that a transferable vote in a matter such as the flag would result in almost no opinion at all or a hodge-podge of opinions. I feel that this would not produce a satisfactory result.
I say that for this reason, and this is my next point. If you have a parliamentary committee to try and arrive at a compromise design, I am sure that this could be done. There have been a number of discussions amongst hon. members, and I am sure a number of hon. members present are aware of them. Several flag designs have been privately and informally discussed. These flag designs might well meet the points of view of quite a number of members on both sides of this house, and might be even more appropriate than some of the designs suggested so far. I will not go into the details of these designs, but many hon. members know to what I am referring. If a parliamentary committee were set up, and if none of the present flag designs could command a majority of public support, the flag designs which are being discussed could present a compromise point of view, would receive a chance for consideration and might meet some mutual point of view.
If such a committee were set up, I suggest of ten members, on which every party had appropriate representation, it would also have to be made clear that the decision of such a committee would not need to be unanimous. Clearly you might run into some maverick or ornery character, to use the vernacular, who would not agree. But if 80 per cent of three quarters of the committee agreed on a design, the design could then be presented to the house for consideration.

Would the hon. member
permit a question?
Certainly.

I am very interested in the suggestions he is making, but what would he suggest the committee do if, for example, as

Canadian Flag
a result of the plebiscite you get 35 per cent of the people for the red ensign, 10 per cent in favour of the red ensign with some modification to indicate the heritages of both founding races, 25 per cent in favour of three maple leaves and 30 per cent in favour of a single maple leaf? It seems to me that we would be in a situation of utter confusion and it would make it very difficult for parliament to act.

I can see very little point in this, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), for whose opinions I have a high degree of respect, did not hear what I said. I said that if none of the designs proved to command even a simple majority of the people of the country, there are a number of other designs which are being promoted here and elsewhere which could be considered. I know a number of people who prefer the red ensign but would accept another design, to which I will not refer at the moment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question.
Yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In that case, if the committee came up with some design other than the four proposed designs, would not that design have to be presented to the country in yet another plebiscite? Would not the same principle which calls for a plebiscite now have to be employed again?
Well, that might well be the case.
Oh, oh.
A plebiscite to the death.
This is one of the problems we have here, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We want to live to see the issue resolved.

I imagine that this is why it is difficult to meet points of view. There may be faults in suggestions which are made, although I do not see any faults in this suggestion; but when suggestions are made in this house hon. members have set views and are not prepared to listen to new ideas. I think that is the case with most of the government members.
Would the hon. member permit still another question?
Yes.

It seems that we are never going to get a vote on the plebiscite question, but I was wondering whether the next suggestion from the opposition might be that we have a plebiscite on whether we should have a plebiscite.
Mr. Speaker, I think everyone is charmed with the wit of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) and would probably be half right.
Would the hon. member permit another question?
No, well, yes, I would be delighted.

I was wondering whether the problem could not be solved by having a plebiscite in which we list the 2,900 designs we have received, and have a transferable, preferential ballot, and then we could give the statistics people ten years off to tabulate the results.
Might I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

My hon. friend is making a very serious speech and I think a helpful one. However, I am sure the hon. member recognizes that the recommendation of the Prime Minister in his resolution is an endeavour to honour what has been an emblem which goes back nearly 100 years. Is it possible that he or any of his associates or colleagues in his part of the house have any ideas how this emblem, which was formally adopted in 1921 under the Meighen government in the reign of King George V, could be preserved in a fashion more acceptable than the resolution presently presented?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is on the coat of arms.

In reply to my hon. friend's question, it could be preserved in the Canadian coat of arms. In reply to the question of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), facetiousness is all good fun and we all enjoy it, and he and the hon. member for York-Scarborough are some sort of twins in this regard, although they are not of the same party. However, in order to finish my remarks I will have to ask hon. members, if they have any more questions, helpful or otherwise-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: -to submit them to a plebiscite.

-to keep them till the end. Regardless of the rather interesting and amus-

ing little interlude we have had through the efforts of the members of the Liberal and New Democratic parties I still believe a parliamentary committee of ten members could arrive at a design acceptable to the house. If the hon. members for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau), Danforth (Mr. Scott) and Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who showed a remarkable sense of humour which I did not think he possessed, would agree, perhaps we could commence with a plebiscite.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Perhaps it was the hon. member who excited it.
I am very glad to have excited something in the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, if I may say that.
Oh, oh.
Be careful.

In any event, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up more than my allotted time as I know there are other members on the government side who wish to speak. I would be very pleased to hear them make some suggestions. I am sure all members would be glad to receive them. I do not believe we have heard from any member of the government party other than the Prime Minister.
Where were you this afternoon?
We did hear something from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), but I do not think he was very helpful.
You were asleep.

I am sorry to have created any difficulty, Your Honour, having promised earlier that I would not make a speech of a provocative nature. However, you will realize that under certain circumstances one must change his intentions.
It has been said that a plebiscite would cost approximately $6 million. That may be the case but there is no reason why such a plebiscite could not be held during the next federal election. No one, except members on the government side, seem to think there is any urgency in this flag matter. I am sure that as long as we have a flag by 1967, which is our 100th birthday, that is all that is necessary. If the government does feel there is a reason for having a flag before 1967, in order perhaps to fulfil the Prime Minister's election campaign promise of two years ago, there is no reason why such a plebiscite could not be held this fall in September or October. Regardless of the $6 million cost, if a referendum
Canadian Flag
assisted in the creation of national unity and obviated the necessity for further divisive debate it would be worth it.
Perhaps we could form a parliamentary committee of the type I have suggested, to arrive at some decision in regard to a national flag within a two year period of time allowing the Prime Minister to fulfil his promise, making everyone happy. I think it is important that this divisive debate taking place both in this house and in the country as a whole be concluded. I expect one of my friends on the government side to say that all we have to do to effect this result is discontinue our remarks, and the debate will conclude. I think that is a correct statement but there is one thing wrong with it. We now have a minority government attempting to force a minority view down the throats of the population of Canada.
How could we do that?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hamilton West, in one of his customary bright interjections has said: "How could we do that?" If my hon. friend from Hamilton West is so sure of his position why does he object to a plebiscite?
Let us vote on it. Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member for Oxford how he thinks a minority government could force anything down the throats of the majority of members?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to make remarks in reference to other parties in the house, but it is suggested that the smaller parties will support the minority government.
The design being proposed by the government is not a design proposed by other parties. Since the Prime Minister has made it very clear in this house that unless his design is supported there will be an election, and since most members of this house, as well as the majority of this country's population, do not want an election at this time, I think the government can expect to receive support from other parties.
Oh, come, come.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?

No, not at the moment.
Mr. Speaker, I hear the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) say, "come, come, come". I do not think my friend wants an election at the present time. I do not think

Canadian Flag
that the majority of the members of this house want an election at this time.

What have you to say
about that which your leader said this afternoon?
I do not know how the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) would know what was said this afternoon. I did not see him in the house during most of this afternoon.
I was here all afternoon, sir.
I do not know where.
Would a free vote help?

I suggest that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) put that suggestion to his leader.
Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned it is the view of the majority of the members of this house that we now face a difficult impasse. This impasse was created by the government.
Oh, oh.

This impasse was created by the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) and by his government.
Regardless of that fact, Mr. Speaker, I have made some attempt this evening to be constructive, although that is very difficult to do at certain times. I suggest the only way out of this very difficult impasse, which exists not only in this house but in this country itself, is to hold a plebiscite. If the results of that plebiscite indicate that a substantial majority is in favour of the proposed flag design then it should be adopted. If a majority indicates a preference for another flag, that flag should be adopted. If only something less than a majority indicates a preference toward any particular design then the matter should be referred to a parliamentary committee. I think that is the
only way of solving this impasse which has. become extremely difficult not only for this house but for the country as a whole. This continued debate is divisive and costly. I do not think any group here will be able to force a view on another. There must be a little give and take on all sides, and I hope all members in this house will realize that fact. I am sorry that some hon. members opposite apparently do not agree.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the flag presently proposed by the government is unfortunately regarded as a partisan flag in a great many places in this country. I agree that perhaps the country as a whole does not take that view. We cannot adopt a flag to represent national unity, our ideals and ambitions for the future, that is in any way regarded as a partisan flag. For that reason I hope that the hon. members of this house will make an attempt to co-operate and perhaps make concessions so that we can make some arrangements for the adoption or retention of a Canadian national flag. I do not suggest that what I have proposed is perfect.
In a rather witty and humorous way a number of members have pointed out some theoretical objections to my proposal, and although I do not feel they are practical, I will admit that there are difficulties. I am not narrow minded in respect of this matter and will be glad to listen to any other suggestions hon. members wish to make, particularly those hon. members on the government side. Someone must make some suggestions if we are to conclude this debate. Members of parties other than the government party have made suggestions. Those suggestions may not be entirely suitable, but as long as the suggestions are being made I think we are progressing.
Mr. Speaker, I see that it is now 10.30 so I will resume my seat.
It being thirty minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.
Wednesday, August 19, 1964
